Fly Ltd. made a sale of INR 7,00,000 to Wings International in May 2023 and recognised Trade Receivables which was initially recorded at the prevailing exchange rate on the date of sales, transaction recorded at US$ 1= ₹79.4. The Company also took a loan from U.S Company for ₹10,00000 in December 2023 which was initially recorded at the prevailing exchange rate on the date of transaction, transaction recorded at US$ 1= ₹81.1.

On 31st March 2024, exchange rate was US$ 1 = ₹83.3.
question_html: What will be the closing balance of Trade Receivables on 31st March 2024:
answer_html: Answer: (C) ₹7,34,383 approx — the trade receivable is a foreign-currency monetary asset, restated at the closing rate on the balance sheet date. USD principal = ₹7,00,000 / 79.4 = USD 8,815.82 (approx); at the closing rate of USD 1 = ₹83.3, the restated balance = 8,815.82 × 83.3 = ₹7,34,383 approx.
chapter_label: AS 11: The Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates
topic_text: AS 11 (3.4): Foreign currency monetary item (trade receivable) restated at the closing rate on the balance sheet date

case_facts_html:
X Ltd. purchased 3,000 shares of Amazing Ltd. in December 2023 @ ₹100 each and paid brokerage @ 1%. In May 2024, Amazing Ltd. issued bonus shares at one for every three shares held by shareholders.

X Ltd. sold 1000 shares in September 2024 at ₹110 each. After issue of bonus, shares were quoted at ₹95. In December 2024, the shares were quoted at ₹70.
question_html: What would be the carrying cost of investments in Amazing Ltd. after sale of shares as per AS 13:
answer_html: Answer: (B) ₹2,27,250 — original cost = 3,000 shares × ₹100 + 1% brokerage = ₹3,03,000. The May 2024 bonus issue (1 for 3) adds 1,000 shares at nil cost, so the weighted-average cost across the enlarged 4,000-share holding remains ₹3,03,000, i.e. ₹75.75/share. On sale of 1,000 shares in September 2024, the cost removed = 1,000 × ₹75.75 = ₹75,750, leaving the carrying cost of the remaining 3,000 shares at ₹3,03,000 − ₹75,750 = ₹2,27,250.
topic_text: AS 13 (3.5): Weighted-average cost per share after a bonus issue, applied to shares sold

case_facts_html:
X Ltd. purchased 3,000 shares of Amazing Ltd. in December 2023 @ ₹100 each and paid brokerage @ 1%. In May 2024, Amazing Ltd. issued bonus shares at one for every three shares held by shareholders.

X Ltd. sold 1000 shares in September 2024 at ₹110 each. After issue of bonus, shares were quoted at ₹95. In December 2024, the shares were quoted at ₹70.
question_html: What is the cost of bonus shares:
answer_html: Answer: (C) Nil — bonus shares are not separately costed; the existing cost of the original holding (₹3,03,000) is simply spread over the enlarged number of shares (original 3,000 plus 1,000 bonus = 4,000), so the bonus shares themselves carry no incremental cost.
topic_text: AS 13 (3.5): Cost of bonus shares is nil, by analogy to AS 13's rights-share cost-spreading principle

case_facts_html: Sun Limited has acquired 40% share in Moon Ltd. for ₹500,000 on 01.07.2023. Moon Ltd. is holding 40% stake in Star Limited. Now, sun limited can exercise significant influence on Moon Limited. Moon limited declared dividend of ₹80,000 for the Financial Year 2022-23 on 15.09.2023. For the year 2023-24, Moon Ltd. earned profit of ₹4,00,000 and declared dividend for ₹90,000 on 15.09.2024.
question_html: With respect to relationship between Companies, it can be said that:

options.A: Star Ltd. is associate of Sun Ltd.
options.B: Moon Ltd. and Star Ltd. both are associates of Sun Ltd.
options.C: Moon Ltd. is an associate of Sun Ltd.
options.D: Sun Ltd. is Parent of both Moon Ltd. and Star Ltd.

answer_html: Answer: (C) Moon Ltd. is an associate of Sun Ltd. — Sun's direct 40% stake in Moon falls within AS 23's significant-influence range (20%-50%), making Moon an associate. Star Ltd. is not itself directly held by Sun; Moon's 40% stake in Star does not, on its own, extend associate status from Sun to Star, since Moon is only an associate (not a subsidiary) of Sun, and AS 23 does not treat an indirect holding routed through another associate as conferring significant influence.
chapter_label: AS 23: Accounting for Investments in Associates in CFS
topic_text: AS 23 (2.3): Associate relationship via direct significant influence; an indirect stake held through another associate does not itself confer associate status

case_facts_html: Sun Limited has acquired 40% share in Moon Ltd. for ₹500,000 on 01.07.2023. Moon Ltd. is holding 40% stake in Star Limited. Now, sun limited can exercise significant influence on Moon Limited. Moon limited declared dividend of ₹80,000 for the Financial Year 2022-23 on 15.09.2023. For the year 2023-24, Moon Ltd. earned profit of ₹4,00,000 and declared dividend for ₹90,000 on 15.09.2024.
question_html: What will be the carrying amount of investment in Separate Financial Statements of Sun Limited as on 31.03.2024?
answer_html: Answer: (C) ₹4,68,000 — in Sun's separate financial statements, the investment is carried at cost. The dividend of ₹80,000 declared on 15.09.2023 relates to Moon's FY2022-23 profits, a pre-acquisition period (Sun acquired its stake on 01.07.2023); Sun's 40% share of this pre-acquisition dividend (₹32,000) is treated as a recovery of the cost of investment, not as income, reducing the carrying cost to ₹5,00,000 − ₹32,000 = ₹4,68,000.
topic_text: AS 13 (3.5): Separate financial statements: a pre-acquisition dividend received is deducted from the cost of investment

case_facts_html: Sun Limited has acquired 40% share in Moon Ltd. for ₹500,000 on 01.07.2023. Moon Ltd. is holding 40% stake in Star Limited. Now, sun limited can exercise significant influence on Moon Limited. Moon limited declared dividend of ₹80,000 for the Financial Year 2022-23 on 15.09.2023. For the year 2023-24, Moon Ltd. earned profit of ₹4,00,000 and declared dividend for ₹90,000 on 15.09.2024.
question_html: What will be the carrying amount of investment in Consolidated Financial Statements of Sun Limited as on 31.03.2024?
answer_html: Answer: (B) ₹5,88,000 — under the equity method for CFS, the carrying amount starts from the same pre-acquisition-dividend-adjusted cost as the separate financial statements (₹4,68,000, see Q3(b)) and is increased by Sun's 40% share of Moon's post-acquisition profit for FY2023-24, time-apportioned for the 9 months since acquisition (01.07.2023 to 31.03.2024): 40% × ₹4,00,000 × 9/12 = ₹1,20,000. Carrying amount = ₹4,68,000 + ₹1,20,000 = ₹5,88,000.
chapter_label: AS 23: Accounting for Investments in Associates in CFS
topic_text: AS 23 (2.6): Equity-method carrying amount: cost net of pre-acquisition dividend plus a time-apportioned share of post-acquisition profit

question_html: As per AS 23, the existence of significant influence by an investor is usually evidenced in one or more of the following ways: (a) participation in policy making processes; (b) interchange of managerial personnel; (c) right to receive dividend; (d) provision of essential technical information.
answer_html: Answer: (D) Statements (a), (b) and (d) are correct — participation in policy-making, interchange of managerial personnel, and provision of essential technical information are all AS 23 evidences of significant influence. A mere right to receive dividend (statement c) is not, since it is a passive entitlement common to any shareholder rather than evidence of participation in decisions.
chapter_label: AS 23: Accounting for Investments in Associates in CFS
topic_text: AS 23 (2.3): Evidences of significant influence under AS 23 - excludes a mere right to receive dividend

question_html: Cost of current investment acquired was ₹1000 but the fair value was ₹800. The Investment was recorded at ₹800. Now the fair value of Investment is Rs 1200. At what value should it be recorded and how much gain will be credited to profit and loss account.

options.A: No change is required and it will continue at ₹800
options.B: Current investment will be recorded at ₹1000 and gain of ₹200 will be credited to profit and loss account.
options.C: Current investment will be recorded at ₹1200 and gain of ₹400 will be credited to profit and loss account.
options.D: Current investment will be recorded at ₹1200 but no gain will be credited to profit and loss account.

answer_html: Answer: (B) Current investment will be recorded at ₹1,000 and gain of ₹200 will be credited to profit and loss account — under AS 13, the investment was initially carried at the lower of cost (₹1,000) and fair value (₹800), i.e. ₹800. When fair value subsequently rises to ₹1,200, the carrying amount can be written back up, but only as far as the original cost (₹1,000) — never above it, even though the new fair value is higher. The write-back from ₹800 to ₹1,000 is a gain of ₹200 credited to profit and loss.
topic_text: AS 13 (3.6): Current investment written up only to original cost, never above cost, even if fair value later exceeds cost

question_html: As per AS 20 an enterprise should present/disclose the following: (a) the amounts used as the numerators in calculating basic and diluted earnings per share, and a reconciliation of those amounts to the net profit or loss for the period. (b) the weighted average number of equity shares used as the denominator in calculating basic and diluted earnings per share, and a reconciliation of these denominators to each other. (c) basic and diluted earnings per share, even if the amounts disclosed are negative (a loss per share). (d) the nominal value of shares along with the earnings per share figures.
answer_html: Answer: (A) All the statements are correct — AS 20 requires disclosure of the numerator amounts and their reconciliation to net profit, the denominator (weighted average shares) and its reconciliation, both basic and diluted EPS even when negative, and the nominal value of shares alongside the EPS figures.
topic_text: AS 20 (5.12): AS 20 mandatory disclosures, including the nominal value of shares alongside EPS figures

question_html: Accounting Standard 10, Property, Plant and Equipment is applicable to:

options.A: Biological Assets (other than Bearer Plants) related to agricultural activity
options.B: Wasting Assets including Mineral rights, Expenditure on the exploration for and extraction of minerals, oil, natural gas and similar non-regenerative resources
options.D: Bearer Plant (except produce on Bearer Plants)

answer_html: Answer: (D) Bearer Plant (except produce on Bearer Plants) — AS 10 covers bearer plants themselves (the produce growing on them is outside AS 10's scope, covered elsewhere), while biological assets generally, wasting assets/mineral rights, and inventories are all excluded from AS 10's scope.
topic_text: AS 10 (2.2): Scope of AS 10 - bearer plants included (produce excluded); biological assets and wasting assets excluded

case_facts_html:
Excellence Ltd. is a Real Estate Company which constructs residential and commercial projects for selling. The Company has commenced a new project and the expenses incurred are as follows:

  • The cost of land acquired for Project is ₹10 crore
  • Cost of construction incurred is ₹25 crores.
  • The Company also incurred cost of ₹10 lacs for various administrative meetings in relation to planning of the building.
  • The construction of building completed and at the end of the year 1, the net realisable value of the building was ₹40 crore.
  • At the beginning of the next year (year 2), the Company decided to use the building as its corporate office.
  • The Company further incurred ₹50 lacs for making necessary changes in the structure for using it as corporate office in accordance with government norms for commercial spaces. Without these changes the office cannot be set up.
  • Ignore the effect of depreciation, if any.

In view of above information, answer the following issues:
question_html: At the end of Year 1, how the building should be classified:
answer_html: Answer: (A) Inventory — Excellence Ltd. is constructing the building to sell, not for own use; while that intention holds, AS 2 governs and the asset is inventory (a completed unit held for sale in the ordinary course of business), regardless of its capital value.
topic_text: AS 2 (1.2): Inventories held for sale in the ordinary course of business - self-constructed real estate for sale is inventory, not PPE

  • Ignore the effect of depreciation, if any.

In view of above information, answer the following issues:
question_html: At the end of Year 1, at value Project should be recognised:
answer_html: Answer: (B) ₹35 Crore — cost = land ₹10 crore + construction ₹25 crore = ₹35 crore; the ₹10 lacs administrative-meeting cost is a general administrative overhead not directly attributable to bringing the inventory to its present condition, so AS 2 excludes it from cost. NRV was ₹40 crore. Inventory is valued at the lower of cost and NRV = ₹35 crore.
topic_text: AS 2 (1.9): Administrative overheads not contributing to location/condition excluded from inventory cost

question_html: At the end of Year 2, the Project should be valued at:

case_facts_html:
Supercool ltd. is a manufacturing company, engaged in manufacturing eco-friendly equipment. On April 1, 2023, the Company received a grant of ₹20 crore from the Government (which is 25% of the total capital of the Company) for various purposes that the company deems fit and no repayment is required to be made to Government.

The Company also borrowed ₹10 crore from financial Institutions and interest paid on the same during the year is ₹1 lac.

The Company acquired plant and machinery from the funds for ₹10 crore and ₹1 crore was spent on its installation and assembly.

₹10 lacs were spent on professional fees necessary for installation and operating of the machine. The Company also spent ₹50 lacs on revenue expenditure.

The Plant and Machinery was ready for its intended use on September 30, 2023.

The depreciation on plant and machinery is charged @10%.
question_html: The grant of ₹20 crores received by the Company should be presented as:

options.B: Grants related to Specific Fixed Assets

answer_html: Answer: (C) Capital Reserve — the ₹20 crore grant is 25% of total capital, is for "various purposes the company deems fit," and carries no repayment obligation or asset-specific condition; this is a grant in the nature of a promoters' contribution, which AS 12 requires to be credited directly to Capital Reserve, not treated as deferred income or netted against a specific asset.
topic_text: AS 12 (1.8): Grants of the nature of promoters' contribution credited to Capital Reserve

case_facts_html:
Supercool ltd. is a manufacturing company, engaged in manufacturing eco-friendly equipment. On April 1, 2023, the Company received a grant of ₹20 crore from the Government (which is 25% of the total capital of the Company) for various purposes that the company deems fit and no repayment is required to be made to Government.

The Company also borrowed ₹10 crore from financial Institutions and interest paid on the same during the year is ₹1 lac.

The Company acquired plant and machinery from the funds for ₹10 crore and ₹1 crore was spent on its installation and assembly.

₹10 lacs were spent on professional fees necessary for installation and operating of the machine. The Company also spent ₹50 lacs on revenue expenditure.

The Plant and Machinery was ready for its intended use on September 30, 2023.

The depreciation on plant and machinery is charged @10%.
question_html: At what value the plant and machinery acquired should be recognised as at 31st March 2024:
answer_html: Answer: (C) ₹10.54 Crore — cost of P&M = purchase price ₹10 crore + installation/assembly ₹1 crore + professional fees necessary for installation/operation ₹10 lacs (₹0.10 crore) = ₹11.10 crore gross (the grant is presented as Capital Reserve, not deducted from the asset, so gross cost is unaffected by it). Ready for intended use 30th September 2023, so FY2023-24 depreciation runs 6 months: ₹11.10 crore × 10% × 6/12 = ₹0.555 crore. Net carrying value = ₹11.10 crore − ₹0.555 crore = ₹10.545 crore ≈ ₹10.54 crore.
topic_text: AS 10 (2.6-2.7): Cost of PPE = purchase price plus directly attributable costs; depreciation time-apportioned from the date ready for intended use

question_html: The revenue expenditure of ₹50 lacs should be recognised as:

options.C: Revenue expenditure in the Profit and Loss

Supercool ltd. is a manufacturing company, engaged in manufacturing eco-friendly equipment. The Company also borrowed ₹10 crore from financial Institutions and interest paid on the same during the year is ₹1 lac.

The Company acquired plant and machinery from the funds for ₹10 crore and ₹1 crore was spent on its installation and assembly.

The Plant and Machinery was ready for its intended use on September 30, 2023.

question_html: Which of the following statement is true:

options.A: Plant and Machinery has been acquired out of Government Grant so the same should be disclosed at Nil value.
options.B: Plant and Machinery belongs to Financial Institution
options.C: Plant and Machinery belong to the Company and should be recognised as its Property, Plant and Equipment

The payment for the buyback will be made using the company's bank balance, which is part of its current assets.

question_html: As per The Companies Act, 2013 under Section 68 (2) the buy-back of shares in any financial year must not exceed

options.A: 20% of its total paid-up capital and free reserves
options.B: 25% of its total paid-up capital and free reserves

answer_html: Answer: (B) 25% of its total paid-up capital and free reserves — Section 68(2)(c) of the Companies Act, 2013 caps buy-back of shares/other specified securities in any financial year at 25% of the aggregate of the company's paid-up capital and free reserves.

question_html: Accounting Standard 19, Lease is applicable on following Leases:

options.A: Lease agreements to explore for or use of natural resources, such as oil, gas, timber metals and other mineral rights.
options.B: Legal owner of an asset conveys to another party in return for a payment or series of periodic payments, the right to use an asset for an agreed period of time.
options.C: licensing agreements for items such as motion picture films, video recordings, plays, manuscripts, patents and copyrights.

answer_html: Answer: (B) — AS 19 defines a lease as the conveyance, by the legal owner of an asset, of the right to use that asset to another party for an agreed period in return for a payment or series of payments; this is the definition itself. Options (A), (C) and (D) are all activities/agreements AS 19 explicitly excludes from its scope (natural-resource exploration/use rights, licensing agreements for films/patents/copyrights, and land lease agreements).

question_html: On 31st March 2024, Sri Radhey shyam Enterprise finds that the cost of a partly finished unit on that date is ₹530. The unit can be finished in 2024-25 by an additional expenditure of ₹310. The finished unit can be sold for ₹750 subject to payment of 8% brokerage on the selling price. Sri Radhey shyam Enterprise seeks your advice regarding the amount at which the unfinished unit should be valued as at 31st March, 2024 for preparation of final accounts. The partly finished unit cannot be sold in semi-finished form and its NRV is zero without processing it further.
answer_html: Answer: (B) ₹380 — estimated selling price when finished ₹750, less further cost to complete ₹310, less 8% brokerage on selling price (8% × ₹750 = ₹60) = Net Realisable Value ₹380. Since the partly finished unit cannot be sold in its semi-finished state (its own NRV is zero without further processing), it is valued with reference to the finished good's NRV net of the cost still to be incurred: ₹750 − ₹310 − ₹60 = ₹380, lower than the ₹530 cost incurred so far, so the unit is valued at ₹380 per AS 2's lower-of-cost-and-NRV rule.
topic_text: AS 2 (1.3): Worked NRV example for a partly finished unit that cannot be sold in semi-finished form

answer_html: Answer: (B) ₹2,17,500 — sale value net of trade discount: 5 × (₹45,000 − ₹500) = ₹2,22,500, less the installation-fee portion (5 × ₹1,000 = ₹5,000) not yet earned as installation was not complete by 31st March — ₹2,22,500 − ₹5,000 = ₹2,17,500.

question_html: Is the Company required to do any accounting for 1-year warranty provided by it:

options.A: No accounting treatment is required till some warranty claim is actually received by the Company.

case_facts_html:
A company engaged in refining, transportation, and marketing of petroleum products, during the financial year ended 31st March, 2025, acquired a controlling interest in another public sector undertaking from the Government of India at ₹1,551 per share. The book value and market value of the shares as of 18th February, 2025 were ₹192.58 and ₹876 per share, respectively. The company paid a strategic premium of ₹675 per share due to various tangible and intangible factors.

The company classified the acquired shares as long-term strategic investments and accounted for them at cost (₹1,551 per share); no provision for diminution in value was made. Schedule III requires the aggregate market value of quoted shares to be disclosed, and this has been reflected. On 28th March, 2025, the market price was ₹880 per share. By 18th July, the price had dropped to ₹300. Management believes the decline is not permanent, given strategic and synergy benefits expected, and hence no provision for diminution has been made.

Based on the information given above, answer Question Nos. 10–13.
question_html: Is the accounting treatment of recording the investment 'at cost' without providing for diminution correct as per AS 13?

options.A: Yes, as the investment is classified as long-term.
options.B: Yes, provided the decline in value is not other than temporary.
options.C: No, the market value must always be considered for long-term investments.
options.D: No, a provision for diminution must be made regardless of the cause of decline.

answer_html: Answer: (B) — AS 13 requires long-term investments to be carried at cost, with a provision only for a decline that is other than temporary; classification as long-term alone does not exempt an entity from testing for a permanent diminution.
topic_text: AS 13 (3.4): Long-term investments carried at cost, written down only for other-than-temporary decline

question_html: P Ltd. has 60% voting right in Q Ltd. Q Ltd. has 20% voting right in R Ltd. Also, P Ltd. directly enjoys voting right of 14% in R Ltd. R Ltd. is a Listed Company and regularly supplies goods to P Ltd. The Management of R Ltd. has not disclosed its relationship with P Ltd. While preparing Financial Statements of P Ltd., which entities would you disclose as related parties with reference to AS-18?

options.D: Neither of Q Ltd. or R Ltd.

answer_html: Answer: (C) Q Ltd. and R Ltd. — Q Ltd. is a subsidiary of P Ltd. (P Ltd. controls >50% of its voting power), a related party outright. AS 18 defines "control"/"substantial interest" as direct or indirect ownership without dilution through a controlled subsidiary — since P Ltd. controls Q Ltd., Q Ltd.'s full 20% stake in R Ltd. is attributed to P Ltd.'s group interest. Combined with the direct 14%, the group holds 34% of R Ltd. — past AS 18's 20% substantial-interest threshold — making R Ltd. a related party too, regardless of R Ltd. management's own non-disclosure.
topic_text: AS 18 (4.3): Significant influence via combined direct and full (non-diluted) indirect voting power held through a controlled subsidiary

question_html: A Machinery was given on 3 years lease by a dealer of the machinery for equal annual lease rentals to yield 20% profit margin on cost of the machinery, which is ₹3,00,000. Economic life of the machinery is 5 years, and estimated output from the machinery in 5 years is: Year I 50,000 units, Year II 60,000 units, Year III 40,000 units, Year IV 65,000 units, Year V 85,000 units. Compute Annual Lease Rent.
answer_html: Answer: (B) ₹60,000. This is an operating lease (the machine returns to the dealer after the 3-year term, with 2 years of economic life remaining). Total amount the dealer targets recovering over the machine's full economic life = cost + 20% margin = ₹3,00,000 × 1.20 = ₹3,60,000, recovered progressively in proportion to how much of the machine's total lifetime output is consumed during each period of use — not amortised flat over just the 3-year lease term. Output during the lease (Years I–III): 50,000+60,000+40,000 = 1,50,000 units, exactly 50% of the machine's total 5-year output (3,00,000 units). The dealer therefore targets recovering 50% of ₹3,60,000 = ₹1,80,000 during this lease, as equal annual rentals: ₹1,80,000 / 3 = ₹60,000/year.
topic_text: AS 19 (5.2): Operating lessor's target rental recovery apportioned by the leased asset's output consumed during the lease term, out of its full economic-life output

case_facts_html:
Sun Limited has acquired 40% share in Moon Ltd. for ₹5,00,000 on 01.07.2024. Moon Ltd. is holding 40% stake in Star Limited. Sun Limited can exercise significant influence on Moon Limited. Moon Limited declared dividend of ₹80,000 for FY 2023-24 on 15.09.2024. For 2024-25, Moon Ltd. earned profit of ₹4,00,000 and declared dividend of ₹90,000 on 15.09.2025.

Answer the following questions based on the above.
question_html: With respect to relationship between Companies, it can be said that:

options.A: Star Ltd. is associate of Sun Ltd.
options.B: Moon Ltd. and Star Ltd. both are associates of Sun Ltd.
options.C: Moon Ltd. is an associate of Sun Ltd.
options.D: Sun Ltd. is Parent of both Moon Ltd. and Star Ltd.

answer_html: Answer: (C) Moon Ltd. is an associate of Sun Ltd. — Sun Ltd. holds 40% (≥20%) of Moon Ltd. with significant influence, making Moon an associate. Star Ltd. is held only indirectly, through Moon (which is itself merely an associate, not a subsidiary, of Sun) — AS 23's associate-via-subsidiary attribution logic does not extend through a non-controlled intermediate, so Star Ltd. is not Sun Ltd.'s associate on these facts.
chapter_label: AS 23: Accounting for Investments in Associates in CFS
topic_text: AS 23 (2.2): Associate relationship does not extend through a non-controlled intermediate holding

question_html: As per AS 23, the existence of significant influence by an investor is usually evidenced in one or more of the following ways: (i) Participation in policy making processes; (ii) Interchange of managerial personnel; (iii) Right to receive dividend; (iv) Provision of essential technical information.
answer_html: Answer: (D) — AS 23 lists board representation, policy-making participation, material inter-company transactions, interchange of managerial personnel, and provision of essential technical information as significant-influence indicators. question_html: Vijay Ltd. borrowed ₹30 lakh at interest rate of 5% per annum and purchased plant and machinery for ₹60 lakh (using borrowed funds) and started production. It took 1 year time for Vijay Ltd. to create optimum market for the goods manufactured and generate revenue. How much borrowing cost can be capitalised with cost of plant and machinery:

question_html: The cost of inventories of items that are not ordinarily interchangeable and goods or services produced and segregated for specific projects should be assigned using the following cost formula:

case_facts_html:
SEAS Ltd., the "Company", is in the business of tours and travels. It sells holiday packages to the customers. The Company negotiates upfront with the Airlines for specified number of seats in flight. The Company agrees to buy a specific number of tickets and pay for those tickets regardless of whether it is able to resell all of those in package.

The rate paid by the Company for each ticket purchased is negotiated and agreed in advance. The Company also assists the customers in resolving complaints with the service provided by airlines. However, each airline is responsible for fulfilling obligations associated with the ticket, including remedies to a customer for dissatisfaction with the service.

The Company bought a forward contract for three months of US$ 1,00,000 on 1 March 2024 at 1 US$ = INR 83.10 when exchange rate was US$ 1 = INR 83.02. On 31 March 2024, when the Company closed its books, exchange rate was US$ 1 = INR 83.15. On 1 April 2024, the Company decided for premature settlement of the contract due to some exceptional circumstances.

The Company is evaluating below mentioned schemes: (i) Introduction of a formal retirement gratuity scheme by an employer in place of ad hoc ex-gratia payments to employees on retirement. (ii) Management decided to pay pension to those employees who have retired after completing 5 years of service in the organization. Such employees will get pension of ₹20,000 per month. Earlier there was no such scheme of pension in the organization.

SEAS Ltd. has a subsidiary, ADI Ltd., which is in the business of construction having turnover of ₹200 crores. SEAS Ltd. and ADI Ltd. hold 9% and 23% respectively in an associate company, ASOC Ltd. Both SEAS Ltd. and ADI Ltd. prepare consolidated financial statements as per Accounting Standards notified under the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2021.
question_html: What would be the basis of revenue recognition for SEAS Ltd. as per the requirements of Accounting Standards?

options.C: Depends on the accounting policy of the Company.
options.D: Indian GAAP allows a choice to the Company to recognize revenue on gross basis or net basis.

answer_html: Answer: (A) Gross basis — per AS 9, whether revenue is recognised gross or net (as a mere commission) turns on who bears the risks and rewards of the transaction. SEAS Ltd. commits upfront to buy a fixed number of tickets and must pay for them regardless of resale, i.e. it bears the inventory/resale risk itself rather than merely arranging a sale on the airline's behalf, so it is a principal, not an agent, and recognises the full amount charged to the customer as revenue.
topic_text: AS 9 (2.3): Agency relationship - gross vs net (commission-only) revenue determined by who bears risks and rewards

question_html: Please suggest accounting treatment of forward contract for the year ended 31 March 2024 as per Accounting Standard 11.

options.A: MTM (marked to market value) of contract will be recorded on 31 March 2024.
options.B: MTM (marked to market value) of contract will be computed as at 31 March 2024 and only if there is loss, it will be recorded during the year ended 31 March 2024.
options.C: No accounting will be done during the year ended 31 March 2024.
options.D: Premium on contract will be amortized over the life of the contract.

answer_html: Answer: (D) Premium on contract will be amortized over the life of the contract — the forward contract was entered into to hedge a foreign-currency risk, not for speculation. Per AS 11, the premium or discount on such a forward exchange contract (the difference between the forward rate and the spot rate at inception: here 83.10 − 83.02 = ₹0.08 per US$) is amortised as expense or income over the life of the contract, while any exchange difference on the contract itself is recognised in profit or loss in the period in which the exchange rate changes.
chapter_label: AS 11: The Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates
topic_text: AS 11 (3.11): Hedging forward exchange contracts - premium/discount amortised over the contract life

question_html: You are requested to advise the Company in respect of the accounting requirements of above schemes related to employee benefits as to which one of those schemes should be considered as a change in accounting policy during the year.

options.A: 1 – Change in accounting policy. 2 – Change in accounting policy.
options.B: 1 – Not a change in accounting policy. 2 – Change in accounting policy.
options.C: 1 – Not a change in accounting policy. 2 – Not a change in accounting policy.
options.D: 1 – Change in accounting policy. 2 – Not a change in accounting policy.

answer_html: Answer: (C) 1 – Not a change in accounting policy. 2 – Not a change in accounting policy. — per AS 5, the adoption of an accounting policy for a transaction/event that did not occur previously, or that previously did not exist, is not a change in accounting policy. Both scheme 1 (formalising ad hoc ex-gratia payments into a retirement gratuity scheme) and scheme 2 (introducing a pension scheme where none existed before) are first-time adoptions for a previously non-existent benefit, not a switch from one existing policy to another, so neither qualifies as a change in accounting policy.
chapter_label: AS 5: Net Profit or Loss, Prior Period Items and Changes in Accounting Policies
topic_text: AS 5 (2.5): Changes in Accounting Policies - first-time adoption for a previously non-existent item is not a policy change

SEAS Ltd. has a subsidiary, ADI Ltd., which is in the business of construction having turnover of ₹200 crores. SEAS Ltd. and ADI Ltd. hold 9% and 23% respectively in an associate company, ASOC Ltd. Both SEAS Ltd. and ADI Ltd. prepare consolidated financial statements as per Accounting Standards notified under the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2021.
question_html: Please comment regarding consolidation requirements for SEAS Ltd. and ADI Ltd. using the below mentioned options as to which one should be correct.

options.A: ADI Ltd. would use equity method of accounting for 23% in ASOC Ltd. SEAS Ltd. would consolidate ADI Ltd. and consequently automatically equity account 23% and separately account for the balance 9% as per AS 13.
options.B: ADI Ltd. would account for 23% in ASOC Ltd. as per AS 13. SEAS Ltd. would consolidate ADI Ltd. and consequently automatically account 23% and separately account for the balance 9%.
options.C: ADI Ltd. would account for 23% share in ASOC Ltd. using equity method of accounting. SEAS Ltd. would consolidate ADI Ltd. and consequently, automatically account for ASOC Ltd. 23% share and separately account for 9% share in ASOC Ltd. using equity method of accounting in consolidated financial statements.
options.D: ADI Ltd. would account for 23% in ASOC Ltd. as per AS 13. SEAS Ltd. would consolidate ADI Ltd. and using equity method of accounting 23% in ASOC Ltd. and separately account for the balance 9% as per AS 13.

answer_html: Answer: (C) — ADI Ltd.'s own 23% direct stake already exceeds the 20% significant-influence threshold, so ADI Ltd. equity-accounts it under AS 23 in its own books; when SEAS Ltd. consolidates its subsidiary ADI Ltd. under AS 21, that 23% equity-accounted stake carries through automatically. Separately, at the group level SEAS Ltd.'s own direct 9% is not tested in isolation — the group's combined effective interest (direct 9% + indirect 23% via the subsidiary = 32%) exceeds 20%, so ASOC Ltd. is an associate of the group as a whole, and SEAS Ltd.'s direct 9% must also be equity-accounted (not treated as a plain AS 13 investment), consistent with AS 23's rule on aggregating direct and indirect holdings through a controlled subsidiary.
chapter_label: AS 23: Accounting for Investments in Associates in CFS
topic_text: AS 23 (2.3): Effective direct-plus-indirect associate holding through an intermediate/controlled subsidiary, tested at the group level

On 1st April, 2022, Shubham Limited purchased some land for ₹30 lakhs for the purpose of constructing a new factory. This cost of ₹30 lakhs included legal cost of ₹2 lakhs incurred for the purpose of acquisition of this land. Construction work could start on 1st May, 2022 and Shubham Limited provides the following details of the costs incurred in relation to its construction:

Particulars₹
Preparation and levelling of the land80,000
Employment costs of the construction workers (per month)29,000
Purchase of materials for the construction21,24,000
Cost of relocating employees to new factory for work60,000
Costs of inauguration ceremony on 1st January, 202380,000
Overhead costs incurred directly on the construction of the factory (per month)25,000

General overhead costs allocated to the construction project by the Manager is ₹30,000. However, as per the company's normal overhead allocation policy, it should be ₹24,000. The auditor of the company has support documentation for the cost of ₹15,000 only, and raised objection for the balance amount.

The construction of the factory was completed on 31st December, 2022 and production could begin on 1st February, 2023. The overall useful life of the factory building was estimated at 40 years from the date of completion. However, it was estimated that the roof will need to be replaced 20 years after the date of completion and that the cost of replacing the roof at current prices would be 25% of the total cost of the building.

The construction of the factory was partly financed by a loan of ₹28 lakhs borrowed on 1st April, 2022. The loan was taken at an annual rate of interest of 9%. During the period when the loan proceeds had been fully utilized to finance the construction, Shubham Limited received investment income of ₹25,000 on the temporary investment of the proceeds.

Assume that all of the net finance costs are to be allocated to the cost of factory (not land) and that interest cost is to be capitalized based on a nine months' period.
question_html: Which of the following cost (incurred directly on construction) will be capitalized to the cost of factory building?
answer_html: Answer: (A) ₹2,00,000 incurred as legal cost, per the Ans.pdf's Division A answer key ("2. (i) (a)").

case_facts_html:
Kesar Ltd., a company engaged in various business activities, has decided to initiate a share buy-back on 1st April, 2023. The company plans to repurchase 25,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at a price of ₹20 per share. This buy-back initiative is in compliance with the company's articles of association, and the necessary resolution has been duly passed by the company. As part of the financial arrangement for the share buy-back, Kesar Ltd. intends to utilize its current assets, particularly the bank balance, to make the payment for the repurchased shares.

Here is a snapshot of Kesar Ltd.'s Balance Sheet as of 31st March, 2023:

Particulars₹
A. Share Capital: Equity share capital (fully paid up shares of ₹10 each)12,50,000
B. Reserves and Surplus: Securities premium2,50,000
   Profit and loss account1,25,000
   Revenue reserve15,00,000
C. Long term borrowings: 14% Debentures28,75,000
   Unsecured Loans16,50,000
D. Land and Building19,30,000
   Plant and machinery18,00,000
   Furniture and fitting9,20,000
   Other Current Assets30,00,000

Authorized, issued and subscribed capital: Equity share capital (fully paid up shares of ₹10 each) – ₹12,50,000.
question_html: By using the Shares Outstanding Test the number of shares that can be bought back:
answer_html: Answer: (B) 31,250 shares — Shares Outstanding Test permits buy-back of up to 25% of the total outstanding equity shares. Outstanding shares = ₹12,50,000 / ₹10 = 1,25,000 shares; 25% of 1,25,000 = 31,250 shares.
topic_text: Buy-back of Securities (1): Shares Outstanding Test - 25% of total outstanding equity shares

question_html: By using the Resources Test determine the number of shares that can be bought back:
answer_html: Answer: (D) 39,062 shares — Resources Test permits buy-back up to 25% of (paid-up capital + free reserves), divided by the buy-back price. Paid-up capital ₹12,50,000 + free reserves (Securities premium 2,50,000 + P&L 1,25,000 + Revenue reserve 15,00,000 = 18,75,000) = ₹31,25,000; 25% = ₹7,81,250; ÷ ₹20/share = 39,062.5, rounded down to 39,062 shares.

question_html: By using the Debt Equity Ratio Test determine the number of shares that can be bought back:
answer_html: Answer: (C) 28,750 shares — post-buy-back debt must not exceed twice post-buy-back (paid-up capital + free reserves). Total debt = 14% Debentures 28,75,000 + Unsecured Loans 16,50,000 = ₹45,25,000; minimum required post-buy-back (capital+free reserves) = 45,25,000 / 2 = ₹22,62,500. Each share bought back reduces combined capital+free reserves by ₹30 (the ₹20 cash outflow, i.e. ₹10 capital + ₹10 premium, plus a further ₹10 nominal value transferred out of free reserves into the non-free Capital Redemption Reserve): 31,25,000 − 30x ≥ 22,62,500 ⇒ x ≤ 8,62,500/30 = 28,750 shares.
topic_text: Buy-back of Securities (1): Debt-Equity Ratio Test - post buy-back debt capped at twice post buy-back paid-up capital and free reserves

question_html: On the basis of all three tests determine Maximum number of shares that can be bought back:
answer_html: Answer: (C) 28,750 shares — the maximum permissible buy-back is the LEAST of the three tests: Shares Outstanding Test 31,250 (Q3(i)), Resources Test 39,062 (Q3(ii)), Debt-Equity Ratio Test 28,750 (Q3(iii)). question_html: All of the following costs are excluded while computing value of inventories except?

options.B: Allocated fixed production overheads based on normal capacity.
options.D: Storage costs (which is necessary part of the production process).

answer_html: Answer: (B) Allocated fixed production overheads based on normal capacity — per AS 2, fixed production overhead systematically allocated on the basis of normal capacity is a genuine, includable cost of conversion, not excluded from inventory value. Selling/distribution costs and abnormal wastage are always expensed, never inventoried.
topic_text: AS 2 (1.6): Fixed production overhead absorbed systematically over normal capacity - includable in cost of conversion

question_html: According to AS-18 Related Party Disclosures, which ONE of the following is not a related party of Skyline Limited?

options.A: A shareholder of Skyline Limited owning 30% of the ordinary share capital.
options.B: An entity providing banking facilities to Skyline Limited in the normal course of business.
options.D: Key management personnel of Skyline Limited.

answer_html: Answer: (B) An entity providing banking facilities to Skyline Limited in the normal course of business — AS 18 specifically excludes providers of finance, utilities, statutory bodies and similar parties from the related-party definition solely because of a normal-course-of-business relationship, even where that relationship involves significant transaction volume, provided there is no economic dependency beyond an ordinary customer/supplier relationship.
topic_text: AS 18 (4.4): Who is NOT deemed a related party under AS 18 - providers of finance/utilities in the normal course of business

question_html: A process of reconstruction, which is carried out without liquidating the company and forming a new one is called

options.C: Amalgamation in the nature of merger.
options.D: Amalgamation in the nature of purchase.

answer_html: Answer: (A) Internal reconstruction — a reorganisation of a company's capital structure and writing-off of accumulated losses without winding up the company or forming a new one, as distinct from external reconstruction/amalgamation which involves liquidating the old company and transferring its business to a new or existing one.
topic_text: Internal Reconstruction (1): Internal reconstruction (no winding up) vs external reconstruction (amalgamation in the nature of merger)

case_facts_html:
Mars Ltd. is a manufacturing enterprise which is starting a new manufacturing plant at X Village. It has commenced construction of the plant on April 1, 2023 and has incurred following expenses: It has acquired land for installing Plant for ₹50,00,000. It incurred ₹35,00,000 for material and direct labour cost for developing the Plant. The Company incurred ₹10,00,000 for head office expenses at New Delhi which included rent, employee cost and maintenance expenditure. The Company borrowed ₹25,00,000 for construction work of Plant @12% per annum on April 1, 2023. Director finance of the Company incurred travel and meeting expenses amounting to ₹5,00,000 during the year for arranging this loan. On November 1, 2023, the construction activities of the plant were interrupted as the local people alongwith the activists have raised issues relating to environmental impact of plant being constructed. Due to agitation the construction activities came to standstill for 3 months. With the help of Government and NGOs, the agitation was over by February 28, 2024 and the work resumed. However, to balance the impact on environment, government ordered the company to install certain devices for which the Company had to incur ₹6,00,000 in March 2024. The rate of depreciation on Plant is 10%.

Based on the above information, answer the following questions.
question_html: Which of the following expenses cannot be included in the cost of plant:
answer_html: Answer: (C) Head office expenses — general administrative overheads (rent, employee cost, maintenance) incurred at the New Delhi head office are not directly attributable to bringing the plant to its location and working condition, so under AS 10 they are excluded from the cost of the plant. Cost of land, direct construction material/labour, and (subject to the capitalisation-period rules tested in Q2) the eligible borrowing cost are all includible.
topic_text: AS 10 (2.6-2.7): Cost of a self-constructed asset - directly attributable costs only, general/HO overhead excluded

question_html: How much amount of borrowing cost can be capitalised with the plant:
answer_html: Answer: (B) ₹2,00,000 — full-year borrowing cost = ₹25,00,000 × 12% = ₹3,00,000. AS 16 requires capitalisation to be suspended during an extended period in which active development is interrupted (the environmental-agitation halt is not a routine, necessary part of the construction process, so it is a genuine suspension, not merely a temporary delay). Treating the suspension as running from 1 November, 2023 to 28 February, 2024 (4 months, per the resumption date actually given), the eligible capitalisation period is the remaining 8 months (April–October, 7 months, plus March, 1 month): ₹3,00,000 × 8/12 = ₹2,00,000.

case_facts_html:
Beloved Finance Ltd. is a financial enterprise which is in the business of lending loan to small businesses and earn interest on loans. During the year the Company has lend 50 crores and earned ₹1.5 crore as interest on loans. The Company had surplus funds during the year and invested then in Fixed Deposits with bank and earned interest on fixed deposits of ₹20 lacs. The Company also acquired a gold loan unit for ₹10 crore during the year and the Company provided interest free loan of ₹15 crore to its wholly-owned subsidiary. The Company paid a total income tax of ₹75 lacs for the year.

Based on the above information, answer the following questions.
question_html: In the Cash Flow Statement as per AS 3, the interest income of ₹1.5 crore earned on loans given by the Company will be disclosed as:
answer_html: Answer: (A) Operating Activities — for a financial enterprise (whose principal revenue-generating activity is lending), interest received on loans made in the ordinary course of business is classified as an operating cash flow, not an investing one.
topic_text: AS 3 (2.4): Interest received by a financial enterprise on its core lending activity is an operating cash flow

case_facts_html:
Kumar Ltd., a privately-held company, operates in the manufacturing industry. Founded in 2008, the company has steadily grown its operations and established a strong presence in the market. As of 31st March, 2023, the company's capital structure reflects a blend of equity and debt financing.

Capital Structure Overview: Equity Share Capital: The company has a total of ₹30,00,000 invested in equity shares, each valued at ₹10 and fully paid. Reserves & Surplus: Kumar Ltd. has accumulated reserves and surplus totaling ₹49,00,000, comprising contributions from various sources including General Reserve (₹32,50,000), Security Premium Account (₹6,00,000), Profit & Loss Account (₹4,30,000), and Revaluation Reserve (₹6,20,000). Loan Funds: The company has acquired loan funds amounting to ₹42,00,000 to support its operational and growth initiatives.

Buy-Back Decision: Considering its financial position and market conditions, Kumar Ltd. has decided to initiate a share buy-back program. The company intends to repurchase its shares at a price of ₹30 per share. In accordance with financial regulations and internal policies, Kumar Ltd. aims to assess the maximum number of shares it can repurchase while maintaining a prudent debt-equity ratio. By utilizing the Debt Equity Ratio Test, the company seeks to strike a balance between its equity base and debt obligations.

Based on the above information, answer the following questions.
question_html: What is the minimum equity Kumar Ltd. needs to maintain after buy-back, according to the Debt Equity Ratio Test?
answer_html: Answer: (B) ₹21,00,000 — the Debt Equity Ratio Test under Section 68(2)(e) of the Companies Act requires post-buy-back debt not to exceed twice the post-buy-back paid-up capital and free reserves (2:1 ratio). With Loan Funds fixed at ₹42,00,000, the minimum equity that must be retained is ₹42,00,000 ÷ 2 = ₹21,00,000.
topic_text: Buy-back of Securities (1): Debt-Equity Ratio Test - post-buyback debt capped at 2x paid-up capital and free reserves

question_html: Sahil Ltd agreed to sell its factory located in Assam to Kali Ltd on 4.12.2023. It entered into a sale deed (transferring all significant risks and rewards of ownership) on 1.2.2024. But the transaction was registered with the registrar on 30.5.2024. When should the sale and gain be recognized?

options.A: Both sale and gain should be recognized as on the balance sheet date i.e. 31.3.2024.
options.B: Both sale and gain should be recognized on 30.5.2024.
options.C:
The sale should be recognized as on balance sheet date but gain should be recognized on
      30.5.2024.
options.D: Both sale and gain should be recognized on 4.12.2023.

answer_html: Answer: (A) — derecognition/disposal of an item of PPE is recognised once significant risks and rewards of ownership have transferred to the buyer (here, via the sale deed executed 1.2.2024, before the 31.3.2024 balance sheet date), not on the later date of formal registration with the registrar, which is a legal formality rather than the substantive transfer event. Since the transfer occurred before the year end, both the sale and the resulting gain are recognised in the financial statements for the year ended 31.3.2024, i.e. as on the balance sheet date.
topic_text: AS 10 (Retirements and De-recognition): Retirements and de-recognition - gain/loss recognised when risks and rewards transfer, not on later legal registration

question_html: Pratham and Associates is a manufacturer of steel rods. It invests its profits by purchasing shares of listed companies in order to earn dividend income. It had purchased shares of Bharti Airtel Limited in FY 2018-19. However, it sold all the shares of Bharti Airtel Limited during the current year i.e. FY 2023-24. What amount would be disclosed in the profit and loss account for FY 2023-24?

options.A:
This transaction would not affect the profit and loss account since the primary business of
      the company is manufacturing, and not investment.
options.B: The carrying amount net of expenses would be disclosed in the profit and loss account.
options.C: The disposal proceeds net of expenses would be disclosed in the profit and loss account.
options.D:
The difference between the carrying amount and the disposal proceeds, net of expenses, would
      be disclosed in the profit and loss account.

answer_html: Answer: (D) — AS 13 requires the profit or loss on disposal of an investment to be recognised as the difference between the disposal proceeds and the carrying amount, net of expenses of disposal, in the profit and loss account. This applies regardless of whether investing is the entity's primary business — a manufacturing company that also holds investments is still subject to AS 13 for those investments.
topic_text: AS 13 (3.8): Disposal of investments - gain/loss is the difference between disposal proceeds and carrying amount, net of expenses

question_html: As per Accounting Standards, difference between the Gross Investment and the present value of Minimum Lease Payments under finance lease (from the standpoint of the lessor) and Unguaranteed Residual Value accruing to the lessor is recorded as
answer_html: Answer: (A) Unearned finance income — per AS 19, this exact difference (Gross Investment less the sum of the present value of MLP and the present value of unguaranteed residual value, both at the interest rate implicit in the lease) is the lessor's unearned finance income, recognised over the lease term on a pattern reflecting a constant periodic rate of return on the net investment.
topic_text: AS 19 (5.8): Lessor's gross investment less net investment equals unearned finance income

case_facts_html:
RTS Ltd, ("RTS" or the "Company"), is engaged in the business of manufacturing of urea, has set up its business in a designated backward area which entitles the company to receive from the Government of India a subsidy of 20% of the cost of investment of manufacturing of equipments/components. The Company has a contract with the Indian Railways for a brake component which is structured such that:

  • The Company’s obligation is to deliver the component to the Railways’ stockyard, while the delivery terms are ex-works, the Company is responsible for engaging a transporter for delivery.
  • Railways sends an order for a defined quantity.
  • The Company manufactures the required quantity and informs Railways for carrying out the inspection.
  • Railways representatives visit the Company’s factory and inspect the components, and mark each component with a quality check sticker.
  • Goods once inspected by Railways, are marked with a hologram sticker to earmark for delivery identification by the customer when they are delivered to the customer’s location.
  • The Company raises an invoice once it dispatches the goods.

The management of RTS is under discussion with the auditors of the Company in respect of accounting of a critical matter as regards its accounting with respect subsequent events i.e. events after the reporting period. They have been checking as to which one of the following events after the reporting period provide evidence of conditions that existed at the end of the reporting period?

  1. Nationalisation or privatization by government
  2. Out of court settlement of a legal claim
  3. Rights issue of equity shares
  4. Strike by workforce
  5. Announcing a plan to discontinue an operation

The Company has received a grant of ₹8 crores from the Government for setting up a factory in a backward area. Out of this grant, the Company distributed ₹2 crores as dividend. The Company also received land, free of cost, from the State Government but it has not recorded this at all in the books as no money has been spent.

RTS has a subsidiary, LPP Media & Creations Ltd (LPP), an advertising agency which prepares and publishes advertisement in newspapers on behalf of its clients. LPP invoices its clients for the commission they are entitled to as well as the media space payable to the newspaper.

Based on the above information, answer the following questions.
question_html: When should RTS Ltd recognize revenue as per the Accounting Standards notified under the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules. Would your answer be different if inspection is normally known to lead to no quality rejections?

options.A: Revenue should be recognized on dispatch of components. The assessment would not change even in case where inspection is normally known to lead to no quality rejections.
options.B: Revenue should be recognized on completion of inspection of components. The assessment would not change even in case where inspection is normally known to lead to no quality rejections.
options.C: Revenue should be recognized on dispatch of components. The assessment would change where inspection is normally known to lead to no quality rejections.
options.D: Revenue should be recognized on delivery of the component to the Railways’ stockyard. The assessment would change where inspection is normally known to lead to no quality rejections.

answer_html: Answer: (B) — Railways’ inspection here is a substantive acceptance gate (physical quality-check sticker plus a separate hologram identification marking applied only after inspection), not a mere pricing formality, so revenue is recognised only on completion of inspection; a historically low/nil rejection rate does not change this, because the inspection remains a real contractual precondition of the buyer’s acceptance, unlike AS 9’s narrow exception for inspections performed solely to fix a contract price.
topic_text: AS 9 (2.8): Goods subject to a substantive buyer inspection/acceptance procedure - revenue recognised on completion of inspection, not dispatch

RTS has a subsidiary, LPP Media & Creations Ltd (LPP), an advertising agency which prepares and publishes advertisement in newspapers on behalf of its clients. LPP invoices its clients for the commission they are entitled to as well as the media space payable to the newspaper.

Based on the above information, answer the following questions.
question_html: In respect of LPP, how should the revenue be recognized as per Accounting Standards?

options.A: LPP should record net amount of commission earned by it.
options.B: LPP should record net amount of commission earned by it and disclose the information about gross income from advertisement through media and preparation of advertisement material as well as payments to media and expenditure incurred for creation of an advertisement in the notes to accounts.
options.C: LPP should record gross income from advertisement through media and preparation of advertisement material and gross amount of payments to media and expenditure incurred for creation of an advertisement.
options.D: LPP may record this on net or gross basis depending on its accounting policy.

answer_html: Answer: (C) — LPP is not a pure facilitating agent: it prepares/creates the advertisement material itself (a value-added service) and invoices clients for the full amount (commission plus media space payable), taking on primary billing/collection responsibility to the client while separately owing the newspaper for media space. Per AS 9’s agency-relationship principle (only a true agent's commission, not the gross proceeds, is revenue — determined by who bears the risks and rewards), LPP's role here indicates it is acting as principal, so gross income and gross media/production costs are both recorded.
topic_text: AS 9 (2.3): Agency relationship - principal-vs-agent determined by who bears risks and rewards, not merely by invoicing pass-through wording

The Company also received land, free of cost, from the State Government but it has not recorded this at all in the books as no money has been spent.

RTS has a subsidiary, LPP Media & Creations Ltd (LPP), an advertising agency which prepares and publishes advertisement in newspapers on behalf of its clients. LPP invoices its clients for the commission they are entitled to as well as the media space payable to the newspaper.

Based on the above information, answer the following questions.
question_html: Please guide the management of RTS Ltd as to which one of the events mentioned above (i to v) after the reporting period provide evidence of conditions that existed at the end of the reporting period?
answer_html: Answer: (B) ii only — the out-of-court settlement of a legal claim (ii) confirms/quantifies a condition (the dispute and its likely outcome) that already existed at the balance sheet date, so it is an adjusting event under AS 4. The Company has a contract with the Indian Railways for a brake component which is structured such that:

  • The Company’s obligation is to deliver the component to the Railways’ stockyard, while the delivery terms are ex-works, the Company is responsible for engaging a transporter for delivery.
  • Railways sends an order for a defined quantity.
  • The Company manufactures the required quantity and informs Railways for carrying out the inspection.
  • Railways representatives visit the Company’s factory and inspect the components, and mark each component with a quality check sticker.
  • Goods once inspected by Railways, are marked with a hologram sticker to earmark for delivery identification by the customer when they are delivered to the customer’s location.
  • The Company raises an invoice once it dispatches the goods.

The management of RTS is under discussion with the auditors of the Company in respect of accounting of a critical matter as regards its accounting with respect subsequent events i.e. events after the reporting period. They have been checking as to which one of the following events after the reporting period provide evidence of conditions that existed at the end of the reporting period?

  1. Nationalisation or privatization by government
  2. Out of court settlement of a legal claim
  3. Rights issue of equity shares
  4. Strike by workforce
  5. Announcing a plan to discontinue an operation

The Company has received a grant of ₹8 crores from the Government for setting up a factory in a backward area. Out of this grant, the Company distributed ₹2 crores as dividend. The Company also received land, free of cost, from the State Government but it has not recorded this at all in the books as no money has been spent.

RTS has a subsidiary, LPP Media & Creations Ltd (LPP), an advertising agency which prepares and publishes advertisement in newspapers on behalf of its clients. LPP invoices its clients for the commission they are entitled to as well as the media space payable to the newspaper.

Based on the above information, answer the following questions.
question_html: Please guide regarding the accounting treatment of both the grants mentioned above in line with the requirements of Accounting Standard 12.

options.A: Distribution of dividend out of grant is correct. In the second case also not recording land in the books of accounts is correct.
options.B: Distribution of dividend out of grant is incorrect. In the second case, not recording land in the books of accounts is correct.
options.C: Distribution of dividend out of grant is correct. In the second case, land should be recorded in the books of accounts at a nominal value.
options.D: Distribution of dividend out of grant is incorrect. In the second case, land should be recorded in the books of accounts at a nominal value.

answer_html: Answer: (D) — a grant received for setting up a factory (a grant related to a specific fixed asset/promoters’-contribution-style capital grant) is not free surplus available for distribution as dividend without regard to AS 12's presentation requirements, so distributing part of it as dividend is incorrect. Separately, a non-monetary asset (land) received free of cost must still be recognised in the books, at a nominal value if no cost was incurred — it cannot simply be left off the balance sheet.
topic_text: AS 12 (1.5): Non-monetary grants recorded at acquisition cost or nominal value if free; grants are not distributable as dividend without regard to AS 12 presentation

  • It incurred ₹35,00,000 for material and direct labour cost for developing the Plant.

  • With the help of Government and NGOs, the agitation was over by February 28, 2024 and the work resumed. However, to balance the impact on environment, government ordered the company to install certain devices for which the Company had to incur ₹6,00,000 in March 2024.
  • The rate of depreciation on Plant is 10%.

Based on the above information, answer the following questions.
question_html: Which of the following expenses cannot be included in the cost of plant:
answer_html: Answer: (C) Head office expenses — general administrative overheads (rent, employee cost, maintenance at New Delhi head office) are not directly attributable to bringing this specific plant to its working condition, so AS 10 excludes them from cost, unlike land acquired for the plant site, direct construction material/labour, and eligible borrowing cost, all of which are directly attributable.
topic_text: AS 10 (2.6-2.7): Cost of a self-constructed asset - directly attributable costs only, general/administrative overheads excluded

question_html: P Ltd. has 60% voting right in Q Ltd. Q Ltd. has 20% voting right in R Ltd. Also, P Ltd. directly enjoys voting right of 14% in R Ltd. R Ltd. is a Listed Company and regularly supplies goods to P Ltd. The Management of R Ltd. has not disclosed its relationship with P Ltd. While preparing Financial Statements of P Ltd., which entities would you disclose as related parties with reference to AS-18?

options.D: Neither of Q Ltd. or R Ltd.

answer_html: Answer: (C) Q Ltd. and R Ltd. — Q Ltd. is a subsidiary of P Ltd. (P Ltd. controls >50% of its voting power), a related party outright. AS 18 attributes Q Ltd.'s full 20% stake in R Ltd. to P Ltd.'s group interest since P Ltd. controls Q Ltd.; combined with P Ltd.'s direct 14%, the group holds 34% of R Ltd. — past AS 18's 20% substantial-interest threshold — making R Ltd. a related party too, regardless of R Ltd. management's own non-disclosure.
topic_text: AS 18 (4.3): Significant influence via combined direct and full (non-diluted) indirect voting power held through a controlled subsidiary

question_html: A Machinery was giver on 3 years lease by a dealer of the machinery for equal annual lease rentals to yield 20% profit margin on cost of the machinery, which is ₹3,00,000. Economic life of the machinery is 5 years, and estimated output from the machinery in 5 years is as follows: Year I 50,000 units, Year II 60,000 units, Year III 40,000 units, Year IV 65,000 units, Year V 85,000 units. Compute Annual Lease Rent.
answer_html: Answer: (B) ₹60,000. This is an operating lease (the machine returns to the dealer after the 3-year term, with 2 years of economic life remaining). Total amount the dealer targets recovering over the machine's full economic life = cost + 20% margin = ₹3,00,000 × 1.20 = ₹3,60,000, recovered progressively in proportion to how much of the machine's total lifetime output is consumed during each period of use. Output during the lease (Years I–III): 50,000+60,000+40,000 = 1,50,000 units, exactly 50% of the machine's total 5-year output (3,00,000 units). The dealer therefore targets recovering 50% of ₹3,60,000 = ₹1,80,000 during this lease, as equal annual rentals: ₹1,80,000 / 3 = ₹60,000/year.
topic_text: AS 19 (5.2): Operating lessor's target rental recovery apportioned by the leased asset's output consumed during the lease term, out of its full economic-life output

question_html: A process of reconstruction, which is carried out without liquidating the company and forming a new one is called

options.C: Amalgamation in the nature of merger.
options.D: Amalgamation in the nature of purchase.

answer_html: Answer: (A) Internal reconstruction — by definition, this reorganises a company's capital/writes off losses without winding up the existing company or forming a new one; external reconstruction and amalgamation both involve liquidating the transferor company(ies) and vesting the business in a new or existing transferee company.

Year 2: The Company incurred development cost for its new product and incurred ₹25,00,000 (at the beginning of the year) and was of the view that it will get the benefits for the next 5 years.

Year 3: During the year, it was found that due to change in government policies, no further benefits will be available to the Company from development cost.

Answer the following questions on the basis of above information.
question_html: At the end of year 2, what will be the value of Intangible Asset of the Company in the financial statements:
answer_html: Answer: (iv) ₹51,50,000 — by end of year 2 the Company carries two separate intangible assets. case_facts_html:
Hello Ltd., a company engaged in various business activities, has decided to initiate a share buy-back on 1st April, 2023. The company plans to repurchase 25,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at a price of ₹20 per share. This buy-back initiative is in compliance with the company's articles of association, and the necessary resolution has been duly passed by the company. As part of the financial arrangement for the share buy-back, Hello Ltd. intends to utilize its current assets, particularly the bank balance, to make the payment for the repurchased shares.

Here is a snapshot of Hello Ltd.'s Balance Sheet as of 31st March, 2023:

LiabilitiesAssets
(A) Share Capital: Equity share capital (fully paid up shares of ₹10 each)₹12,50,000Land and Building₹19,30,000
(B) Reserves and Surplus: Securities premium₹2,50,000Plant and machinery₹18,00,000
    Profit and loss account₹1,25,000Furniture and fitting₹9,20,000
    Revenue reserve₹15,00,000Other Current Assets₹30,00,000
(C) Long term borrowings: 14% Debentures₹28,75,000
    Unsecured Loans₹16,50,000
Total₹76,50,000Total₹76,50,000

Authorized, issued and subscribed capital: Equity share capital (fully paid up shares of ₹10 each) – ₹12,50,000 (i.e. 1,25,000 shares).

Answer the following questions on the basis of above information.
question_html: By using the Resources Test determine the number of shares that can be bought back:
answer_html: Answer: (iv) 39,062 shares — Section 68(2)(c) caps the buy-back amount (in rupees) at 25% of paid-up capital plus free reserves. Paid-up capital ₹12,50,000 + free reserves (securities premium ₹2,50,000 + P&L ₹1,25,000 + revenue reserve ₹15,00,000 = ₹18,75,000) = ₹31,25,000. 25% of ₹31,25,000 = ₹7,81,250. At the ₹20 buy-back price, this funds 7,81,250/20 = 39,062.5 shares, rounded down to 39,062 whole shares.
topic_text: Buy-back of Securities (1): Resources Test - 25% cap on buy-back value against paid-up capital plus free reserves

Answer (per source answer key): (iii) 28,750 shares.

Flagged, not silently resolved: applying the standard Debt-Equity Ratio Test formula – post buy-back borrowed funds (secured 14% Debentures ₹28,75,000 + Unsecured Loans ₹16,50,000 = ₹45,25,000 total, unaffected by the buy-back) must not exceed twice the post buy-back paid-up capital plus free reserves – gives: maximum permissible reduction in capital+free reserves = ₹31,25,000 − (₹45,25,000/2) = ₹31,25,000 − ₹22,62,500 = ₹8,62,500, i.e. 8,62,500/20 = 43,125 shares at the ₹20 buy-back price. This independently-derived figure (43,125) does not match any of the four printed options, and does not reconcile to the source's own stated letter (iii) 28,750 under this standard method. The discrepancy could not be resolved by re-checking the balance sheet figures (which are internally consistent and balance to ₹76,50,000 on both sides) or by varying which reserves are included (the same ₹31,25,000 capital+free-reserves figure that correctly reproduces part (b)'s Resources Test answer was used here). Kept the source's literal letter as data-answer per the never-silently-fix rule, but this sub-part's own figure–and part (d)'s, which depends on it–should be revisited by Pranav rather than trusted as independently verified.

question_html: As per AS 2, Inventories include materials awaiting use in production process, what should be included in Inventories from the following:

options.A: Secondary Packing material required for transporting and forwarding the material.
options.B: Spare parts, servicing equipment and standby equipment
options.C: Primary packing material which is essential to bring an item of inventory to its saleable condition, for example, bottles, cans etc., in case of food and beverages industry.

answer_html: Answer: (iii) — primary packing material essential to bring an item to its saleable condition (e.g. bottles/cans for food and beverages) is directly attributable to bringing inventory to its present condition and so is includible in inventory cost. Secondary packing (transport/forwarding) is a distribution cost, spare parts/servicing/standby equipment are ordinarily property, plant and equipment rather than inventory, and publicity material is a selling cost – none of these three are inventory.
topic_text: AS 2 (1.2): Primary packing material essential to saleable condition is inventory; secondary packing, standby equipment and publicity material are not

question_html: Sargam Ltd. (the lessee) has taken machinery on lease from Dhun Ltd. (the lessor) for 13 years on annual lease payment of ₹50,000. The life of the machine is 15 years. How this lease arrangement should be classified and why:

options.A: Operating lease because lease payments are being made annually and the value of asset is not available.
options.B: Finance Lease because lease term is for the major part of the economic life of the asset even if title is not transferred.
options.C: Operating Lease because it is not stated that the asset will transferred to lessee at the end of lease term.
options.D: Finance Lease because the leased asset is of a specialized nature such that only the lessee can use it without major modifications being made.

answer_html: Answer: (ii) — AS 19 lists "the lease term is for the major part of the economic life of the asset even if title is not transferred" as one of the situations that would normally lead to a lease being classified as a finance lease. Here the lease term (13 years) is 13/15 ≈ 87% of the machine's 15-year economic life, clearly the major part, so this is the correct classification and reasoning; options (A) and (C) reach the wrong conclusion (operating lease), and (D) reaches the right conclusion for the wrong reason (specialised-nature indicator is not supported by any fact given in the question).
topic_text: AS 19 (5.2): Finance lease indicator - lease term for the major part of the asset's economic life

question_html: Suman Ltd. acquired 1000 shares of Sarika Ltd @ ₹150 each and paid brokerage @ 1%. In the same financial year, Sarika Ltd. issued bonus shares at one share for every four shares held by shareholders. Suman Ltd. sold 500 shares in the month of March in the same year and paid 1% brokerage, what will be the carrying value of investment in Sarika Ltd after sale of shares as per AS 13.
answer_html: Answer: (iii) ₹90,900 — cost of original acquisition including brokerage = 1,000 × ₹150 × 1.01 = ₹1,51,500. Bonus issue of 1 share per 4 held adds 250 shares at nil additional cost, so the holding becomes 1,250 shares at the same total cost of ₹1,51,500 (average cost per share = ₹1,51,500/1,250 = ₹121.20). AS 13 does not recognise a separate cost for bonus shares – the total cost is simply re-averaged over the enlarged holding. After selling 500 shares (brokerage on the sale affects the sale proceeds/profit figure, not the carrying cost of the remaining shares), the remaining 750 shares carry forward at average cost: 750 × ₹121.20 = ₹90,900.
topic_text: AS 13 (3.5): Bonus shares added at nil cost, re-averaging total cost over the enlarged holding, then valuing the remaining balance after a partial sale

case_facts_html:
Health India Limited (HIL), incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013, is engaged in the production and distribution of medicines. It has manufacturing plants at Baddi (Himachal Pradesh) and Bhopal (Madhya Pradesh). It also imports medicines from Pharma Inc. New York (United States).

On 1st Jan 2024, HIL sold 2,00,000 strips of Medicine to Dee Limited for ₹50 Lakhs on 60 days of credit. Cost per strip of this medicine, was ₹20 (i.e. total cost ₹40 Lakhs, 2,00,000 strips @ ₹20). Dee Ltd. paid 20% of the amount due on 5th January, 2024. In March 2024, Dee Limited is having significant cash flow issues and is trying to raise funds through bank loan to run its operations. However, it is unable to do so and not able to release payment to HIL on due date. Subsequent to this, it has gone under liquidation on 15th March, 2024. At the time when medicine was sold by HIL to Dee Limited, there was no reason for HIL to believe that it will not be able to collect the sales proceeds from Dee Limited in future.

On 1st April, 2023 HIL has made an investment of ₹200 Lakhs in the equity shares of Rose Limited of which 50% is made in the long-term category i.e. long-term investment and rest as temporary investment i.e. current investment. The realisable value of all such investments on 31st March, 2024 becomes ₹50 Lakhs as Rose Limited lost a copyright. From the given market conditions, it is apparent that the reduction in the value of investment is not temporary in nature.

HIL imported medicine from Pharma Inc. for a sum of US $2,50,000 on 1st January, 2024. HIL released full payment on 17th April, 2024 to Medicine Ltd. The exchange rates are as follows: 1st April, 2023 ₹76 per $; 1st January, 2024 ₹81 per $; 31st March, 2024 ₹80 per $; 17th April, 2024 ₹79 per $.

HIL is working on a strategic plan to close the production unit of Bhopal due to change in technology. The board of directors approved the closure of Bhopal Plant on 1st March, 2024. The company did a formal announcement regarding closure to the affected parties on 10th March, 2024. The company entered into a binding-sale agreement on 21 April, 2024.

Reporting date of the company is 31st March, 2024. Based on the information given in the above Case Scenario, answer Question Nos. 6–9.
question_html: How the recognition of revenue from sales of medicine to Dee Limited will be done by HIL under AS 9 and what would be the treatment of unrealized amount for the year ended 31st March, 2024?

options.A: Revenue will be recognised for ₹ 50 Lakhs, subsequently unrealized amount ₹ 50 lakhs will be debited to bad debts A/c.
options.B: Revenue will be recognised for ₹ 40 Lakhs, subsequently unrealized amount ₹ 40 lakhs will be debited to bad debts A/c.
options.C: Revenue will be recognised for ₹ 50 Lakhs, subsequently unrealized amount ₹ 40 lakhs will be debited to bad debts A/c.
options.D: Revenue will be recognised for ₹ 40 Lakhs, unrealised amount of ₹ 40 lakhs will be shown in Sundry Debtors list.

answer_html: Answer: (C)
topic_text: AS 9 — Revenue Recognition (2.9): Effect of uncertainties on revenue recognition - post-sale collectability uncertainty
