question_html: P Ltd. has 60% voting right in Q Ltd. Q Ltd. has 20% voting right in R Ltd. Also, P Ltd. directly enjoys voting right of 14% in R Ltd. R Ltd. is a Listed Company and regularly supplies goods to P Ltd. The Management of R Ltd. has not disclosed its relationship with P Ltd. While preparing Financial Statements of P Ltd., which entities would you disclose as related parties with reference to AS-18?

options.D: Neither of Q Ltd. or R Ltd.

answer_html: Answer: (c) Q Ltd. and R Ltd. — Q Ltd. is a subsidiary of P Ltd. (P Ltd. controls >50% of its voting power), so Q Ltd. is a related party outright. AS 18 defines both "control" and "substantial interest" as direct or indirect ownership of the relevant voting-power threshold — since P Ltd. controls Q Ltd. outright, Q Ltd.'s full 20% voting stake in R Ltd. is attributed to P Ltd.'s group interest without dilution (indirect holdings through a controlled subsidiary are not multiplied through the parent's ownership percentage). Combined with P Ltd.'s own direct 14%, the group holds 34% of R Ltd. — well past AS 18's 20% substantial-interest/significant-influence threshold — making R Ltd. a related party too, regardless of R Ltd. management's own non-disclosure.
topic_text: AS 18 (4.3): Significant influence via combined direct and full (non-diluted) indirect voting power held through a controlled subsidiary

answer_html: Answer: (B) Capital reserve — this grant is expressed as a percentage of total investment needed for the factory (a promoter's-contribution-style grant), not tied to any specific fixed asset or revenue item; AS 12 requires such grants to be credited to Capital Reserve, neither treated as deferred income nor distributable as dividend.
topic_text: AS 12 (1.8): Grant in the nature of promoters' contribution (percentage of total investment) credited to Capital Reserve

case_facts_html:
Venus Limited received a parcel of land at no cost from the government for the purpose of developing a factory in an outlying area. The land is valued at ₹75 lakhs, while the nominal value is ₹10 lakhs. Additionally, the company received a government grant of ₹30 lakhs, which represents 25% of the total investment needed for the factory development. Furthermore, the company received ₹15 lakhs with the stipulation that it be used to purchase machinery. There is no expectation from the government for the repayment of these grants.

Answer the following questions based on the above information.
question_html: As per AS 12, how the Government Grant of ₹15 Lakhs with a condition to purchase machinery may be presented as:

options.D: Income in statement of profit and loss as received.

answer_html: Answer: (C) Deferred Income — this grant is tied to a specific depreciable fixed asset (machinery); AS 12 permits presenting such a grant as deferred income, recognised in profit and loss on a systematic basis over the asset's useful life (the alternative being to deduct it from the asset's gross value).
topic_text: AS 12 (1.6): Grant related to a specific fixed asset presented as deferred income

question_html: Which of the above grants are required to be recognised in the statement of profit and loss on a systematic and rational basis over the useful life of the asset:

options.C: Government Grant of ₹15 Lakhs with a condition to purchase machinery

topic_text: AS 12 (1.6): Only the specific-asset-linked grant is amortised to P&L over useful life

case_facts_html:
Axis limited is a manufacturing company. It purchased a machinery costing ₹10 Lakhs in April 2023. It paid ₹4 lakhs upfront and paid the remaining ₹6,00,000 as deferred payment by paying instalment of ₹1,05,000 for the next 6 months. During the year, the Company sold a land which was classified as its ‘property, plant and equipment’ for ₹25,00,000 and paid ₹1,00,000 as income tax as long term capital gain on such sale. During the year, the Company also received income tax refund along with interest.

Answer the following questions based on the above information.
question_html: As per the requirements of AS 3, ‘Cash Flow Statements’, how the amount for purchase of machinery should be presented:

options.A: ₹10 lakhs as ‘Cash flows from Investing Activities’ and ₹30,000 will simply be booked in profit and loss with no presentation in Cash Flow Statement.
options.B: ₹10.30 lakhs as ‘Cash flows from Investing Activities’ as entire amount is spend on purchase of machinery.
options.C: ₹10 lakhs as ‘Cash flows from Investing Activities’ and ₹30,000 as ‘Cash flows from Financing Activities’.
options.D: ₹10.30 lakhs as ‘Cash flows from Financing Activities’ as the machinery has been purchased on finance.

answer_html: Answer: (C) ₹10 lakhs as Investing Activities and ₹30,000 as Financing Activities — the cash price of ₹10 lakhs is the investing outflow for acquiring the fixed asset; the extra ₹30,000 paid under the deferred-instalment terms (6 × ₹1,05,000 = ₹6,30,000 vs. ₹6,00,000 cash-price-equivalent of the deferred portion) is a finance charge, classified as a financing activity, not part of the investing outflow.
topic_text: AS 3 (2.3): Deferred-credit asset purchase split between investing (cash price) and financing (interest element)

case_facts_html:
Axis limited is a manufacturing company. It purchased a machinery costing ₹10 Lakhs in April 2023. It paid ₹4 lakhs upfront and paid the remaining ₹6,00,000 as deferred payment by paying instalment of ₹1,05,000 for the next 6 months. Answer the following questions based on the above information.
question_html: At what amount, the machinery should be recognised in the financial statements:
answer_html: Answer: (D) ₹10,00,000 — per AS 10, the cost of an asset acquired on deferred settlement terms is its cash price equivalent; any excess of the total payments over the cash price is a finance/interest charge, recognised as an expense over the credit period, not capitalised as part of the asset's cost.
topic_text: AS 10 (2.6-2.7): Asset acquired on deferred credit terms recognised at cash price equivalent, excess treated as interest

Axis limited is a manufacturing company. It purchased a machinery costing ₹10 Lakhs in April 2023. During the year, the Company also received income tax refund along with interest.

Answer the following questions based on the above information.
question_html: How should the income tax paid on sale of land should be disclosed in the Cash Flows Statement:

options.D: No disclosure in Cash Flow Statement

answer_html: Answer: (B) Cash flows from Investing Activities — AS 3's general rule classifies taxes on income as operating activities unless the tax can be specifically identified with a financing or investing transaction; here the ₹1,00,000 tax is explicitly identified as capital-gains tax on the land sale (an investing transaction), so it is classified under investing activities along with the sale proceeds.
topic_text: AS 3 (2.3): Tax specifically identifiable with an investing transaction classified under investing activities

question_html: How should the interest on income tax refunds should be disclosed in the Cash Flows Statement:

options.D: No disclosure in Cash Flow Statement

answer_html: Answer: (B) Cash flows from Investing Activities — interest received is, for a non-financial enterprise, classified as an investing activity cash inflow under AS 3, regardless of the fact that it arises on a tax refund.
topic_text: AS 3 (2.5): Interest received classified as an investing activity

question_html: Gyan Ltd. borrowed ₹10 crore for construction of a plant at the rate of 10% per annum (interest paid annually ₹1 crore). The construction was being carried on and out of the borrowings, ₹4 crore was temporarily placed in a fixed deposit at the rate of 6% per annum (interest earned ₹24 lakh). At the year end, how much cost of borrowing Gyan Limited will capitalise?

options.A: Interest paid on ₹10 crore i.e. ₹1 crore
options.B: Interest paid on ₹6 crore as only this amount was utilized i.e. ₹60 Lakh.
options.C: Interest paid less income on temporary investment i.e. ₹76 lakh

answer_html: Answer: (C) ₹76 lakh — per AS 16, borrowing costs eligible for capitalisation are the actual borrowing costs incurred on the specific borrowing, reduced by any income earned on the temporary investment of those funds pending expenditure on the qualifying asset: ₹1,00,00,000 − ₹24,00,000 = ₹76,00,000.
topic_text: AS 16 (4.5): Borrowing cost capitalised net of income on temporary investment of surplus specific-borrowing funds

question_html: Cost of current investment acquired was ₹1,00,000 but the fair value was ₹80,000. The Investment was recorded at ₹80,000. Now the fair value of Investment is ₹1,20,000. At what value should it be recorded and how much gain will be credited to profit and loss account.

options.A: No change is required and it will continue at ₹80,000
options.B: Current investment will be recorded at ₹1,00,000 and gain of ₹20,000 will be credited to profit and loss account.
options.C: Current investment will be recorded at ₹1,20,000 and gain of ₹40,000 will be credited to profit and loss account.
options.D: Current investment will be recorded at ₹1,20,000 but no gain will be credited to profit and loss account.

answer_html: Answer: (B) Recorded at ₹1,00,000, gain of ₹20,000 credited to P&L — AS 13 carries current investments at the lower of cost and fair value; a rise in fair value above cost is never recognised (prudence), so the carrying amount can be written back up only as far as original cost (₹1,00,000), not to the full ₹1,20,000 fair value. The gain recognised (₹1,00,000 − ₹80,000 = ₹20,000) is simply the reversal of the earlier write-down, not an unrealised gain above cost.
topic_text: AS 13 (3.6): Current investment carrying value write-back capped at original cost, never above cost

question_html: In determining the cost of inventories, it is appropriate to exclude certain costs and recognise them as expenses in the period in which they are incurred. Which of the following is not an example of such costs:

options.A: Abnormal amounts of wasted materials, labour, or other production costs;
options.B: Storage costs, unless the production process requires such storage;

answer_html: Answer: (C) Raw Material cost — per AS 2, abnormal wastage, unnecessary storage costs, and selling/distribution costs are all specifically excluded from the cost of inventories and expensed as incurred. Raw material cost, by contrast, is a normal, properly includible component of inventory cost – it is the one item among the four that is not an example of a cost to be excluded.
topic_text: AS 2 (1.9): Exclusions from the cost of inventories – abnormal waste, unnecessary storage, selling/distribution costs

case_facts_html:
Anshul manufacturers purchased 20,000 Kg. of raw material at ₹170 per Kg. Direct transit cost incurred ₹5,00,000 and normal transit loss is 3%. Anshul manufacturers actually received 19,000 kg of raw material. During the year it consumed 17,600 kg of raw material.

Further information: (i) The purchase price includes ₹15 per kg as GST in respect of which full credit is allowed and will be availed by Anshul manufacturers. (ii) Assume that there is no opening stock.

Answer the following questions based on above.
question_html: What will be the cost of material:
answer_html: Answer: (A) ₹36,00,000 — purchase price net of the recoverable GST component: (₹170−₹15) × 20,000 kg = ₹31,00,000, plus direct transit cost ₹5,00,000 = ₹36,00,000. The ₹15/kg GST is excluded from cost since full input tax credit is available (AS 2 excludes duties/taxes subsequently recoverable from the taxing authority).
topic_text: AS 2 (1.5): Cost of purchase excludes recoverable GST, includes directly attributable acquisition costs

Anshul manufacturers purchased 20,000 Kg. of raw material at ₹170 per Kg. Direct transit cost incurred ₹5,00,000 and normal transit loss is 3%. Anshul manufacturers actually received 19,000 kg of raw material. During the year it consumed 17,600 kg of raw material.

Further information: (i) The purchase price includes ₹15 per kg as GST in respect of which full credit is allowed and will be availed by Anshul manufacturers. (ii) Assume that there is no opening stock.

Answer the following questions based on above.
question_html: What will be the value of the closing stock:
answer_html: Answer: (D) ₹2,59,700 — closing stock quantity = actual received 19,000 kg − consumed 17,600 kg = 1,400 kg, valued at the derived cost per kg of ₹185.5 (see Q3): 1,400 × ₹185.5 = ₹2,59,700.
topic_text: AS 2 (1.4): Closing stock valued at cost per kg derived after normal loss absorption

case_facts_html:
Anshul manufacturers purchased 20,000 Kg. of raw material at ₹170 per Kg. Direct transit cost incurred ₹5,00,000 and normal transit loss is 3%. Anshul manufacturers actually received 19,000 kg of raw material. During the year it consumed 17,600 kg of raw material.

Further information: (i) The purchase price includes ₹15 per kg as GST in respect of which full credit is allowed and will be availed by Anshul manufacturers. (ii) Assume that there is no opening stock.

Answer the following questions based on above.
question_html: What will be the cost per Kg of raw material:
answer_html: Answer: (C) ₹185.5 — normal transit loss = 3% of 20,000 kg = 600 kg, so normal expected receipt = 19,400 kg. Cost per kg = ₹36,00,000 ÷ 19,400 kg = ₹185.5 (normal loss is absorbed into the cost of the remaining good units, per AS 2).
topic_text: AS 2 (1.4): Normal loss absorbed into the cost of remaining good units, abnormal loss excluded

topic_text: AS 2 (1.9): Abnormal waste excluded from inventory cost, expensed to P&L

Equity Share Capital of ₹10 each8,000
Capital Redemption Reserve1,000

case_facts_html:
On April 1, 2022, Hello Limited approached a software company for implementation of SAP ERP at its organisation. The cost of implementation of SAP ERP is ₹25,00,000 and the time required is 15 months. The company was also required to pay ₹1,00,000 annually after implementation for maintenance and normal updation of ERP. The implementation work started in June, 2022 and could not be finished in 15 months. The ERP was implemented on May 2024. Due to delay in implementation the vendor refunded ₹2,00,000. The Company recognised the intangible asset ‘SAP ERP’ on September 2023 (15 months from June 2022). After two years, the Company has got the SAP ERP more upgraded with latest version and additional features and functions which also increased its speed and usage to Hello Limited for ₹7,00,000.

Answer the following questions based on above.
question_html: On which date the Intangible asset should be recognised:

options.A: April 2022 (When it was decided that SAP ERP is to be implemented)
options.C: September 2023 (When the implementation work should have completed as per agreed terms)
options.D: May 2024 (When the SAP actually got implemented)

answer_html: Answer: (D) May 2024 — per AS 26, an intangible asset is recognised only once it is ready for its intended use, i.e. when it is actually available for use, not on the decision date, the start-of-work date, or a contractually-agreed target completion date that was in fact missed.
topic_text: AS 26 (6.19-6.23): Intangible asset recognised on actual readiness for intended use, not a decision or target date

Answer the following questions based on above.
question_html: At what amount the SAP ERP should be initially recognised as ‘intangible asset’:
answer_html: Answer: (C) ₹23,00,000 — implementation cost ₹25,00,000 less the ₹2,00,000 vendor refund for the delay = ₹23,00,000. The refund is a reduction of the acquisition cost, not separate income, since it directly relates to the asset's acquisition.
topic_text: AS 26 (6.7-6.11): Initial cost of a purchased intangible net of a vendor refund for delay

question_html: How should the annual maintenance and updation expenses should be accounted for:

options.B: Should be recognised as a separate ‘Intangible Asset’
options.C: Should be recognised as expense in Profit and Loss annually.

answer_html: Answer: (C) Recognised as expense in Profit and Loss annually — routine maintenance/updation merely preserves the asset's existing level of performance rather than generating benefits in excess of its originally assessed performance, so it fails AS 26's subsequent-expenditure capitalisation test and is expensed as incurred.
topic_text: AS 26 (6.18): Subsequent expenditure expensed unless it generates benefits beyond originally assessed performance

case_facts_html:
On April 1, 2022, Hello Limited approached a software company for implementation of SAP ERP at its organisation. The implementation work started in June, 2022 and could not be finished in 15 months. The ERP was implemented on May 2024. Due to delay in implementation the vendor refunded ₹2,00,000. The Company recognised the intangible asset ‘SAP ERP’ on September 2023 (15 months from June 2022). After two years, the Company has got the SAP ERP more upgraded with latest version and additional features and functions which also increased its speed and usage to Hello Limited for ₹7,00,000.

Answer the following questions based on above.
question_html: During the implementation period, how the expenditure incurred will be accounted for:

options.A: It will be expensed in profit and loss as and when incurred
options.B: It will be recognised as an asset ‘Intangible asset under development’
options.C: It will only be disclosed in notes to accounts and will be recognised when complete
options.D: It will be recognised as an item of Property, Plant and Equipment

answer_html: Answer: (B) Recognised as an asset ‘Intangible asset under development’ — expenditure incurred while the asset is still being implemented (not yet ready for intended use) is accumulated as an intangible asset under development, analogous to capital-work-in-progress for tangible assets, and reclassified once the recognition criteria are met.
topic_text: AS 26 (6.16): Cost accumulated as intangible asset under development during the implementation period

question_html: Vijay Ltd. borrowed ₹30 lakh at interest rate of 5% per annum and purchased plant and machinery for ₹60 lakh (using borrowed funds) and started production. It took 1 year time for Vijay Ltd. to create optimum market for the goods manufactured and generate revenue. How much borrowing cost can be capitalised with cost of plant and machinery:
answer_html: Answer: (C) Nil — the plant was ready for use and production started immediately; it does not become a qualifying asset merely because it took time to build a market for the output, so no borrowing cost is capitalised.
topic_text: AS 16 (4.1): Not a qualifying asset merely because time is needed to build a market for the output

question_html: The cost of inventories of items that are not ordinarily interchangeable and goods or services produced and segregated for specific projects should be assigned using following cost formula

options.A: By specific identification of their individual costs
options.D: The formula used should reflect the fairest possible approximation to the cost incurred in bringing the items of inventory to their present location and condition.

answer_html: Answer: (A) Specific identification of their individual costs — AS 2 requires this for items that are not ordinarily interchangeable, or goods/services produced and segregated for specific projects; FIFO/weighted-average apply only to ordinarily-interchangeable inventory items.
topic_text: AS 2 (1.10): Specific identification for non-interchangeable items and project-specific goods

question_html: Securities held as stock-in-trade held by an entity are:

options.C: May or may not be Investments

answer_html: Answer: (B) Not Investments — AS 13 defines Investments as assets held for earning income (dividends/interest/rentals), capital appreciation, or other benefits, not for trading. Securities held as stock-in-trade are held for sale in the ordinary course of business and fall under AS 2 (inventory), not AS 13.
topic_text: AS 13 (3.1-3.2): Securities held as stock-in-trade are excluded from the definition of Investments

case_facts_html:
Year 1

  • Mr. Lal purchased 1,000 equity shares of ₹100 each in a X Company @ ₹125 each from a stock broker who charged 2% brokerage. At the end of year 1 the market value of these shares is ₹1,50,000. He incurred 50 paise per ₹100 as cost of shares transfer stamps.
  • He also purchased gold for ₹5,00,000 for holding for long term perspective and by year end its value became ₹5,50,000.

Year 2

  • X Company issued bonus shares in the ratio of 1:1. At the end of year 2 market value of 2,000 shares of X Ltd. (including bonus shares) is still ₹1,50,000.
  • At the end of year 2, value of gold purchased is ₹6,50,000.
  • Mr. Lal sold the bonus shares for ₹110 per share during the year.

Answer the following questions on the basis of above information.
question_html: At the end of year 1, what will be the value of the investment in equity shares in the financial statements:
answer_html: Answer: (A) ₹1,28,125 — cost of investment = purchase price (1,000 × ₹125 = ₹1,25,000) + brokerage @2% (₹2,500) + share transfer stamp duty @0.5% of purchase price (₹625) = ₹1,28,125. Per AS 13, a long-term investment is carried at this cost even though the year-end market value (₹1,50,000) is higher — unrealised gains on long-term investments are never recognised.
topic_text: AS 13 — Accounting for Investments (3.5/3.6): Cost of investment includes incidental acquisition charges; long-term investments carried at cost

case_facts_html:
Year 1

  • Mr. Lal purchased 1,000 equity shares of ₹100 each in a X Company @ ₹125 each from a stock broker who charged 2% brokerage. At the end of year 1 the market value of these shares is ₹1,50,000. He incurred 50 paise per ₹100 as cost of shares transfer stamps.
  • He also purchased gold for ₹5,00,000 for holding for long term perspective and by year end its value became ₹5,50,000.

Year 2

  • X Company issued bonus shares in the ratio of 1:1. At the end of year 2 market value of 2,000 shares of X Ltd. (including bonus shares) is still ₹1,50,000.
  • At the end of year 2, value of gold purchased is ₹6,50,000.
  • Mr. Lal sold the bonus shares for ₹110 per share during the year.

Answer the following questions on the basis of above information.
question_html: At the end of year 2, what will be the value of the investment in equity shares in the financial statements:
answer_html: Answer: (A) ₹1,28,125, per the answer key. A pro-rata (cum-bonus) cost-averaging treatment of the 1:1 bonus issue — spreading the original ₹1,28,125 cost over the enlarged 2,000-share holding (₹64.0625/share) and removing the cost of the 1,000 bonus shares sold during the year — would instead value the remaining 1,000-share holding at ₹64,062.50, which is not among this sub-question's own printed options. The letter (A) is reproduced verbatim from the source answer key; see the extraction-note for the unresolved tension this created.
topic_text: AS 13 — Accounting for Investments (3.5/3.6): Carrying value of remaining holding after a bonus issue and part-disposal

Year 2

Answer the following questions on the basis of above information.
question_html: At the end of year 2, what will be the value of the investment in Gold in the financial statements:
answer_html: Answer: (A) ₹5,00,000 — gold held for long-term investment purposes is a long-term investment under AS 13, carried at cost. Since its value has moved favourably (upward, not a decline), there is no basis to write it down, and AS 13 does not permit writing a long-term investment up to a higher market value either. It therefore remains at its original cost.
topic_text: AS 13 — Accounting for Investments (3.6): Long-term investments carried at cost regardless of favourable market movement

  • At the end of year 2, value of gold purchased is ₹6,50,000.
  • Mr. Lal sold the bonus shares for ₹110 per share during the year.

Answer the following questions on the basis of above information.
question_html: How much profit was earned on sale of bonus shares by Mr. Lal:
answer_html: Answer: (C) ₹45,937.50 — under the pro-rata (cum-bonus) cost-averaging treatment, the original cost of ₹1,28,125 is spread evenly over the enlarged 2,000-share holding once the 1:1 bonus is received, giving a cost of ₹64.0625 per share (i.e. half the original cost, ₹64,062.50, notionally attributable to the 1,000 bonus shares). Profit on sale of the 1,000 bonus shares @₹110 = sale proceeds ₹1,10,000 − apportioned cost ₹64,062.50 = ₹45,937.50.
topic_text: AS 13 — Accounting for Investments (3.5): Cost of a bonus issue apportioned pro-rata across the enlarged holding, not treated as nil

case_facts_html: A Company acquired an asset for ₹60 Lakhs with useful life for 10 years. The remaining useful life of the asset now is 4 years and the current carrying amount is ₹30 Lakhs which includes an upward revaluation of ₹6 Lakhs done in the asset last year. Recoverable amount from the asset is 20 Lakhs.
question_html: At what value the asset will be carried in the balance sheet after considering above facts:
answer_html: Answer: (C) ₹20,00,000 — per AS 28, once an asset's carrying amount (₹30 Lakhs) exceeds its recoverable amount (₹20 Lakhs), an impairment loss is recognised and the asset is written down to the recoverable amount itself, i.e. ₹20,00,000.
topic_text: AS 28 — Impairment of Assets (7.7): Carrying amount written down to recoverable amount when impaired

case_facts_html: A Company acquired an asset for ₹60 Lakhs with useful life for 10 years. The remaining useful life of the asset now is 4 years and the current carrying amount is ₹30 Lakhs which includes an upward revaluation of ₹6 Lakhs done in the asset last year. Recoverable amount from the asset is 20 Lakhs.
question_html: What is the amount of impairment loss charged to the statement of profit and loss:
answer_html: Answer: (D) ₹4 Lakhs — total impairment loss = carrying amount ₹30 Lakhs − recoverable amount ₹20 Lakhs = ₹10 Lakhs. Per AS 28, an impairment loss on a revalued asset is first adjusted against that asset's own revaluation reserve (here ₹6 Lakhs, the upward revaluation done last year); only the excess, ₹10 Lakhs − ₹6 Lakhs = ₹4 Lakhs, is charged to the statement of profit and loss.
topic_text: AS 28 — Impairment of Assets (7.7): Impairment loss on a revalued asset set off against revaluation reserve first, excess to P&L

case_facts_html: A Company acquired an asset for ₹60 Lakhs with useful life for 10 years. The remaining useful life of the asset now is 4 years and the current carrying amount is ₹30 Lakhs which includes an upward revaluation of ₹6 Lakhs done in the asset last year. Recoverable amount from the asset is 20 Lakhs.
question_html: What is the amount of depreciation to be charged to the statement of profit and loss after considering above facts:
answer_html: Answer: (A) ₹5 Lakhs — after impairment, the asset's revised carrying amount (₹20 Lakhs) is depreciated over its remaining useful life (4 years): ₹20 Lakhs ÷ 4 = ₹5 Lakhs per year.
topic_text: AS 28 — Impairment of Assets (7.7): Post-impairment depreciation over the remaining useful life

question_html: What is the amount of revaluation reserve in respect of this asset:
answer_html: Answer: (A) Nil — the asset's entire ₹6 Lakh revaluation reserve was fully absorbed in writing off part of the ₹10 Lakh impairment loss (per part (b)), leaving no revaluation reserve balance remaining for this asset.
topic_text: AS 28 — Impairment of Assets (7.7): Revaluation reserve fully extinguished when an impairment loss equals or exceeds it

case_facts_html:
Gases Ltd. is installing a 2000 kms long gas pipeline for distribution of gasses (Project is a qualifying asset as per AS 16). For this purpose it borrowed funds for ₹700 Lakhs at subsidised rates and has to pay annually an interest of ₹70 Lakhs. The Company has also invested unused funds and is earning an income of ₹7 Lakhs annually. During the next year the Company used all funds and no income is now being earned.

During the year 5, the Company has completed 1 stretch of 100 kms which is operational between two points and is capable of intended use.
question_html: For the year 1, how much borrowing cost should be capitalised to the project:
answer_html: Answer: (C) ₹63 Lakhs — per AS 16, income earned on the temporary investment of surplus borrowed funds (before they are actually deployed) is deducted from the borrowing cost eligible for capitalisation. Year 1 interest ₹70 Lakhs − temporary-investment income ₹7 Lakhs = ₹63 Lakhs.
topic_text: AS 16 — Borrowing Costs (4.5/4.6): Eligible borrowing cost net of temporary-investment income before funds are deployed

question_html: For the year 5, how much borrowing cost should expensed:
answer_html: Answer: (C) ₹3.5 Lakhs — per AS 16, when a part of a qualifying asset is completed and capable of being used while construction continues on the rest, capitalisation of the borrowing cost relating to that completed part ceases. topic_text: AS 16 — Borrowing Costs (4.10/4.11): Cessation of capitalisation for a physically completed part of a qualifying asset

question_html: State which of the following statements is true?

options.A:
Buy-back is for more than twenty-five per cent of the total paid-up capital and free
      reserves of the company.
options.B: Partly paid shares cannot be bought back by a company.
options.C:
Buy-back of equity shares in any financial year shall exceed twenty-five per cent of its
      total paid-up equity capital in that financial year.
options.D: Partly paid shares can be bought back by a company.

answer_html: Answer: (B) — Section 68 of the Companies Act, 2013 permits buy-back only of fully paid-up shares; partly paid-up shares are never eligible. Options A and C misstate the statutory caps as floors ("more than"/"shall exceed" 25%, when the Act actually caps buy-back at 25%, not requires it to exceed that), and option D directly contradicts the fully-paid-up requirement.
topic_text: Buy-back of Securities (1): Only fully paid-up securities are eligible for buy-back

question_html: As per AS 19, unearned finance income is:

options.A:
the difference between (a) the gross investment in the lease and (b) the present value of
      minimum lease payments under a finance lease from the standpoint of the lessor; and any unguaranteed
      residual value accruing to the lessor, at the interest rate implicit in the lease.
options.B:
the payments over the lease term that the lessee is, or can be required, to make excluding
      contingent rent, costs for services and taxes to be paid by and reimbursed to the lessor.
options.C:
the aggregate of the minimum lease payments under a finance lease from the standpoint of
      the lessor and any unguaranteed residual value accruing to the lessor.
options.D: the lease is the gross investment in the lease less unearned finance income.

answer_html: Answer: (A) — this is AS 19's own definition of unearned finance income. Option B actually defines "minimum lease payments," option C defines "gross investment in the lease," and option D describes "net investment in the lease" (gross investment less unearned finance income), not unearned finance income itself.
topic_text: AS 19 — Leases (5.3): Definition of unearned finance income

question_html: Akash Ltd. is constructing a housing society and for this purpose, it has taken loan from a bank. The housing society consists of 50 units, each of which can be used individually. 20 units have been constructed and can be opened up for public, while construction on the remaining part is continuing. How much borrowing cost should be capitalised:

options.A:
Capitalisation of borrowing cost should continue for the whole society until construction
      continues.
options.B:
Capitalisation of the borrowing costs shall cease to be capitalised for 20 units which are
      now ready to be used and should continue for 30 units.
options.C: The entire borrowing cost should be capitalised at the end of the project.
options.D: The Borrowing cost will not be capitalised at all.

answer_html: Answer: (B) — per AS 16, when parts of a qualifying asset are capable of being used independently while construction continues on other parts (here, each housing unit can be used individually), capitalisation ceases for the parts substantially complete and ready for use (the 20 units) and continues only for the parts still under construction (the 30 units).
topic_text: AS 16 — Borrowing Costs (4.11): Cessation of capitalisation for independently usable completed parts of a qualifying asset

case_facts_html:
ADI Ltd (the Company), engaged in the business of manufacturing of urea, has set up its business in a designated backward area which entitles the company to receive from the Government of India a subsidy of 20% of the cost of investment.

Having fulfilled all the conditions under the scheme, the Company on its overall investment of ₹50 crores received ₹10 crores from the Government in January 2024 (financial year being 2023-24). The Company wants to treat this receipt as an item of revenue and thereby reduce the losses on profit and loss account for the year ended 31 March 2024.

ADI Ltd holds 51% in SHA Ltd. SHA Ltd is a joint venture of ADI Ltd due to a contractual agreement. ADI Ltd is engaged in the manufacturing business and it entered into a joint venture to get synergies in the same business. ADI Ltd and SHA Ltd hold 10% and 30% respectively in SHB Ltd.

As per the requirements of SEBI, ADI Ltd prepared results/accounts for the quarter ended 30 June 2024 and took following positions in respect of following accounting matters:

  1. Training expenses incurred during the quarter ended 30 June 2024 were allocated equally over the four quarters because the benefit was spread over the entire year and similarly some training expenses expected to be incurred in the last quarter have been estimated and equally allocated over the four quarters.
  2. Provision made for donation of ₹5 million expected to be made in the second quarter.
  3. Since historically there has been an immaterial variance between budgets and actuals, depreciation charge for the quarter was determined by the budgeted figure.
  4. Incentives were provided to the customers if they purchase 1 million kgs of urea on an annual basis. It was expected that at least 50 customers would be able to achieve this target before the end of third quarter. No provision was made for this incentive during the quarter ended 30 June 2024 since ADI Ltd believed that the provision was not yet fructified.

ADI Ltd owns 60% holding in ANI Ltd, an unquoted entity. The government has recently announced an increase in interest rates. The increase will cause a fall in value of equity holdings. This is due to the fact that risk free investments offer a higher return making them relatively more attractive. The market value of equity will adjust downwards to improve the return available on this sort of investment.

SHB Ltd took a loan of USD 10,000 on 1 April 2023 for a specific project at an interest rate of 5% p.a. payable annually. On 1 April 2023, the exchange rate between the currency was ₹81 per USD. The exchange rate as at 31 March 2024 was ₹82 per USD. The corresponding amount could have been borrowed by SHB Ltd in local currency at an interest rate of 11% per annum as on 1 April 2023.

ADI Ltd follows April to March as the financial year.
question_html: In respect of abovementioned receipt of ₹10 crores, which of the following options would be correct under Indian GAAP?

options.A: Accounting treatment desired by the company is correct.
options.B: The subsidy should be credited to capital reserve.
options.C: The subsidy should be treated as a capital grant.
options.D: The accounting treatment should be as per the accounting policy of the company in relation to any grant. The company can choose any accounting policy in this respect.

answer_html: Answer: (B) — the subsidy is calculated as 20% of the Company's total investment (₹50 crores), not tied to the cost of any one specific depreciable fixed asset, and is received only after the Company fulfils backward-area investment conditions. This is the classic AS 12 fact pattern for a "government grant of the nature of promoters' contribution" — such a grant is credited directly to Capital Reserve and treated as part of shareholders' funds, never recognised as revenue/P&L income (so the Company's own desired treatment, option (A), is wrong).
topic_text: AS 12 (1.8): Investment subsidy tied to total investment (not a specific depreciable asset) is credited to Capital Reserve as promoters' contribution, not recognised as revenue

question_html: Please suggest which one of the following options would be correct in respect of consolidated accounts of ADI Ltd as per Accounting Standards notified under the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules.

options.A: In the consolidated accounts of ADI Ltd, it would account for its 10% investment in SHB Ltd as per AS 13 and 30% investment of SHA Ltd in SHB Ltd would be accounted for using equity method.
options.B: In the consolidated accounts of ADI Ltd, it would account for its 10% investment in SHB Ltd as per equity method and 30% investment of SHA Ltd in SHB Ltd would be accounted using proportionate consolidation method.
options.C: In the consolidated accounts of ADI Ltd, it would account for its 10% investment in SHB Ltd as per AS 13 and 30% investment of SHA Ltd in SHB Ltd would be accounted using proportionate consolidation method.
options.D: In the consolidated accounts of ADI Ltd, it would account for its 10% investment in SHB Ltd as per equity method and 30% investment of SHA Ltd in SHB Ltd would also be accounted for using equity method.

answer_html: Answer: (D) — at the ADI Group's consolidated level, ADI's own direct 10% stake and SHA's 30% stake in SHB Ltd represent a single reporting entity's combined ownership interest in SHB (10% + 51% economic interest in SHA's 30% ≈ 25%+ effective exposure), which crosses the 20% significant-influence threshold in aggregate, with SHA's board seats and business synergies giving the wider group real participation in SHB's policy decisions. On that basis, SHB is treated as an associate of the ADI Group as a whole and equity-accounted for both stakes in the consolidated statements.
chapter_label: AS 23: Accounting for Investments in Associates in CFS
topic_text: AS 23 (2.3): Group's combined direct and indirect (through a jointly-controlled entity) interest assessed together for significant influence in consolidated accounts

question_html: Please share your views in respect of the accounting positions taken by ADI Ltd (Points i to iv) as per Accounting Standards notified under the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules.

options.A: Position taken in point ii was incorrect.
options.B: Positions taken in points ii and iv were incorrect.
options.C: Positions taken in points i and ii were incorrect.
options.D: Positions taken in points i, ii, iii and iv were incorrect.

answer_html: Answer: (D) — all four interim-quarter positions are flawed: (i) training costs create no asset, so smoothing them (including estimated future-quarter training cost) equally across all four quarters is not appropriate merely because "benefit is spread over the year"; (ii) a donation not yet made, with no present obligation existing at quarter-end, cannot be provided for in advance of the obligating event; (iii) interim depreciation must be computed on the actual asset base for the period, not substituted with a budgeted figure, however historically close budget-to-actual has been; (iv) since the Company itself expects at least 50 customers to hit the volume target before quarter three, a proportionate share of the expected incentive cost linked to sales already made in the quarter should be accrued as those sales occur, not deferred until the target has "fructified."
topic_text: AS 25 (7.11): Costs incurred unevenly (training, donation provision, budgeted depreciation, incentive accrual) evaluated against interim-period recognition principles

question_html: Will there be any adjustment required in the financial statements of ADI Ltd because of abovementioned event (increase in interest rates by the Government) as per Accounting Standards notified under the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules.

options.A: The increase is an indication that ADI Ltd's holding in ANI Ltd might have increased. Hence ADI Ltd would require to increase the value of its interest in ANI Ltd.
options.C: The increase is an indication that ADI Ltd's holding in ANI Ltd might be impaired. ADI Ltd should make a formal estimate of the recoverable amount of its interest in ANI Ltd.
options.D: Whether to make any adjustment or not will depend on the accounting policy of ADI Ltd.

answer_html: Answer: (C) — a rise in interest rates makes competing risk-free investments relatively more attractive, pushing the market value of an unquoted equity holding like ANI Ltd downward. This is a classic external indicator of impairment under AS 28: it does not automatically write anything down, but it does trigger a duty to formally estimate the recoverable amount of the interest and test for impairment.
topic_text: AS 28 (7.3): Interest-rate rise indicating possible impairment of an unquoted equity holding triggers a formal recoverable-amount estimate, not an automatic write-up

case_facts_html:
ADI Ltd (the Company), engaged in the business of manufacturing of urea, has set up its business in a designated backward area which entitles the company to receive from the Government of India a subsidy of 20% of the cost of investment.

Having fulfilled all the conditions under the scheme, the Company on its overall investment of ₹50 crores received ₹10 crores from the Government in January 2024 (financial year being 2023-24). The Company wants to treat this receipt as an item of revenue and thereby reduce the losses on profit and loss account for the year ended 31 March 2024.

ADI Ltd holds 51% in SHA Ltd. SHA Ltd is a joint venture of ADI Ltd due to a contractual agreement. ADI Ltd is engaged in the manufacturing business and it entered into a joint venture to get synergies in the same business. ADI Ltd and SHA Ltd hold 10% and 30% respectively in SHB Ltd.

As per the requirements of SEBI, ADI Ltd prepared results/accounts for the quarter ended 30 June 2024 and took following positions in respect of following accounting matters:

  1. Training expenses incurred during the quarter ended 30 June 2024 were allocated equally over the four quarters because the benefit was spread over the entire year and similarly some training expenses expected to be incurred in the last quarter have been estimated and equally allocated over the four quarters.
  2. Provision made for donation of ₹5 million expected to be made in the second quarter.
  3. Since historically there has been an immaterial variance between budgets and actuals, depreciation charge for the quarter was determined by the budgeted figure.
  4. Incentives were provided to the customers if they purchase 1 million kgs of urea on an annual basis. It was expected that at least 50 customers would be able to achieve this target before the end of third quarter. No provision was made for this incentive during the quarter ended 30 June 2024 since ADI Ltd believed that the provision was not yet fructified.

ADI Ltd owns 60% holding in ANI Ltd, an unquoted entity. The government has recently announced an increase in interest rates. The increase will cause a fall in value of equity holdings. This is due to the fact that risk free investments offer a higher return making them relatively more attractive. The market value of equity will adjust downwards to improve the return available on this sort of investment.

SHB Ltd took a loan of USD 10,000 on 1 April 2023 for a specific project at an interest rate of 5% p.a. payable annually. On 1 April 2023, the exchange rate between the currency was ₹81 per USD. The exchange rate as at 31 March 2024 was ₹82 per USD. The corresponding amount could have been borrowed by SHB Ltd in local currency at an interest rate of 11% per annum as on 1 April 2023.

ADI Ltd follows April to March as the financial year.
question_html: Compute the borrowing cost which can be capitalized in the books of SHA Ltd as per the above mentioned fact pattern.
answer_html: Answer: (A) ₹41,000 — the only fact pattern in this case scenario giving loan/interest-rate figures is the USD 10,000 loan taken by SHB Ltd at 5% p.a. (question stem literally says "books of SHA Ltd," see the note below). Plain interest cost = USD 10,000 × 5% = USD 500, converted at the closing/payment-date rate of ₹82/USD = ₹41,000. The exchange-difference-as-interest-cost-adjustment mechanism (which would add the ₹10,000 exchange loss, or cap the total at the ₹89,100 local-currency-equivalent interest) is an optional accounting policy election under AS 11's long-term-monetary-item provisions, not the automatic default — since nothing in the facts states the company elected that treatment, only the plain interest (₹41,000) is the borrowing cost eligible for capitalisation.
topic_text: AS 16 (4.3): Exchange difference on foreign-currency borrowing capitalised as an interest adjustment only via the AS 11 election; absent that, only the plain interest is a borrowing cost

case_facts_html:
SBHA Ltd deals in business of manufacturing, purchase and sale of rice. The company has around 56 acres of land as part of its property, plant and equipment which is stated at cost in its financial statements. As per the new business model, 30 acres of land falls in the residential zone which the company is planning to develop residential area as a plotted development and would like to sell the plots after development.

The company does not have intention of keeping the property development as a business on long-term basis, as the company does not have any objective to receive any income in the form of the capital appreciation or rent as per the proposed business plan and the company wants to sell the plots after development (irrespective of the construction of houses on land).

SBHA Ltd has two equal joint venturers holding 50% each, KSJ one of them. The other company is from outside the KSJ Group. KSJ Group has three companies (one of them is KSJ Ltd and two more companies), each of which hold some equity shares in the joint venture which aggregates 50%.

One of the KSJ Group of companies, ADK Ltd, is engaged in generation of power which is supplied to various Electricity Boards. One of the terms and conditions of the Tariff Regulatory Authority and the tariff agreement is that the income tax relating to the power generating schemes will be reimbursed by the Electricity Boards on quarterly basis before the payment of advance income tax.

RIMMI Ltd, another KSJ Group company, is into shipping business and has an annual turnover of ₹1,000 crores. It is required by law to bring all its vessels into dry dock every five years for major overhaul. This cost is incurred to get the vessel back to its seaworthy condition. A vessel costs ₹20 crores with a useful life of 20 years and it requires major overhaul every 5 years. The estimated cost of first overhaul is ₹5 crores.

In the previous year, RIMMI Ltd had impaired one of its Cash Generating Units (CGU) for a loss of ₹100 crores, with ₹50 crores allocated to goodwill and the balance allocated to Plant & Machinery and Technical Knowhow for a loss of ₹26 crores and ₹24 crores respectively. Recoverable amount was not measurable. Carrying amounts at the end of current year after impairment of ₹100 crores recorded in previous year were ₹427 crores and ₹383 crores for Plant & Machinery and Technical Knowhow respectively. Had there been no impairment in the previous year, the carrying amounts at the end of current year would have been ₹450 crores and ₹405 crores for Plant & Machinery and Technical Knowhow respectively. During the current year, the impairment test proves that the CGU is no longer impaired.
question_html: In respect of abovementioned land in residential zone, what would be the accounting treatment under Indian GAAP?

options.A: The 'land in residential zone' appearing in property, plant and equipment would be credited by its carrying amount and inventory would be recognised equivalent to its fair value. Differential will be taken to profit or loss on conversion.
options.B: The 'land in residential zone' appearing in property, plant and equipment would be credited by its gross amount and inventory would be recognised equivalent to carrying amount of reclassified property, plant and equipment. Differential will be taken to profit or loss on conversion.
options.C: The 'land in residential zone' appearing in property, plant and equipment would be credited by its carrying amount and inventory would be recognised at the same amount.
options.D: The 'land in residential zone' appearing in property, plant and equipment would be credited by its gross amount and inventory would be recognised at the same amount.

answer_html: Answer: (C) — once management's intention changes to selling the plotted land rather than using it operationally, it is reclassified from PPE to inventory. Reclassification itself is not a disposal or a remeasurement event, so no gain/loss is recognised at the point of transfer — the land leaves PPE at its existing carrying amount and enters inventory at that same amount; only on eventual sale is any profit recognised.
topic_text: AS 10 (2.3): Land held for sale as plotted development reclassified from PPE to inventory at carrying amount, with inventory recognised at the same amount

question_html: In the above mentioned situation, how would SBHA Ltd be accounted for by joint venturers as per Accounting Standards notified under the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules?

options.A: Joint venture will be proportionately consolidated by KSJ Ltd only and other venturer outside KSJ Group.
options.B: Joint venture will be proportionately consolidated only by venturer outside KSJ Group.
options.C: Joint venture will be proportionately consolidated by all the three companies of KSJ Group only, to the extent of their own holding.
options.D: Joint venture will be proportionately consolidated by all the three companies of KSJ Group, to the extent of their own holding and other venturer outside KSJ Group (assuming each one has individual control)

answer_html: Answer: (D) — the KSJ Group's collective 50% stake in the SBHA joint venture is actually split across three separate legal entities within KSJ Group, each individually a co-venturer holding its own slice. AS 27's proportionate-consolidation rule applies venturer by venturer, to each venturer's own individual interest — not the group's combined interest as a single block. So each of the three KSJ Group companies proportionately consolidates its own individual share into its own separate financial statements, and the outside venturer does the same for its 50%.
chapter_label: AS 27: Financial Reporting of Interests in Joint Ventures
topic_text: AS 27 (1): Proportionate consolidation applies venturer by venturer to each entity's own individual interest, not to a group's combined interest as one block

question_html: How should the above mentioned transaction in relation to ADK Ltd be accounted for as per Accounting Standards notified under the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules?

options.A: Reimbursement should be recorded as revenue.
options.B: Reimbursement should be taken to other income.
options.C: Reimbursement should be netted from income tax provision.
options.D: Reimbursement can be netted from appropriate expense head like rates & taxes.

answer_html: Answer: (A) — under the Tariff Regulatory Authority's own tariff agreement, the reimbursement of income-tax cost is a contractually built-in part of the price ADK Ltd is entitled to charge the Electricity Boards for the power it supplies. Being an integral, assured component of the regulated tariff for services rendered, it is recognised as revenue, not netted against the unrelated tax-provision or expense line items.
topic_text: AS 9 (2.7): Tariff-linked income-tax reimbursement received as part of the regulated power-tariff mechanism is revenue, not a tax-provision offset

question_html: What should be the accounting treatment in the statement of profit and loss of RIMMI Ltd in year 1 in respect of property, plant and equipment?

options.A: Overhauling costs of ₹5 crores and depreciation of ₹1 crore would be charged to the statement of profit and loss in year 1.
options.B: Depreciation of ₹2 crores would be charged to the statement of profit and loss in year 1.
options.C: Overhauling costs of ₹5 crores and depreciation of ₹75 lakhs would be charged to the statement of profit and loss in year 1.
options.D: Depreciation of ₹1.75 crores would be charged to the statement of profit and loss in year 1.

answer_html: Answer: (D) ₹1.75 crores — per AS 10's component approach, the anticipated first-overhaul cost of ₹5 crores is carved out as a separate component of the vessel with its own 5-year useful life (to the next overhaul), depreciated at ₹5cr ÷ 5 = ₹1 crore/year. The remaining vessel component (₹20cr − ₹5cr = ₹15cr) is depreciated over the full 20-year life at ₹15cr ÷ 20 = ₹0.75 crore/year. Total Year 1 depreciation = ₹1 crore + ₹0.75 crore = ₹1.75 crores; no ₹5 crore expense is charged in Year 1 since the actual overhaul has not yet occurred, only its component is being depreciated in advance.
topic_text: AS 10 (2.10): Major inspection/overhaul cost capitalised as a separate component with its own depreciation period, not expensed when incurred

question_html: What should be the accounting treatment in the books of RIMMI Ltd in respect of impairment of CGU?

options.B: Reversal of impairment loss should be taken to P&L amounting to ₹100 crores.
options.C: Reversal of impairment loss should be taken to P&L amounting to ₹45 crores.
options.D: Reversal of impairment loss should be taken to P&L amounting to ₹50 crores.

answer_html: Answer: (C) ₹45 crores — AS 28 permits reversal of a prior impairment loss on Plant & Machinery and Technical Knowhow (never on goodwill, whose ₹50 crore impairment is permanent), capped at what each asset's carrying amount would have been (net of depreciation/amortisation) had no impairment ever been recorded. Plant & Machinery: ₹450cr (no-impairment hypothetical) − ₹427cr (actual current carrying amount) = ₹23cr reversible. Technical Knowhow: ₹405cr − ₹383cr = ₹22cr reversible. Total reversal = ₹23cr + ₹22cr = ₹45 crores.
topic_text: AS 28 (7.13): Impairment reversal permitted for non-goodwill CGU assets, capped at the no-impairment carrying amount; goodwill impairment is never reversed

case_facts_html:
Asteria Ltd., a listed company with equity share capital of ₹6,000 lakh and free reserves of ₹10,000 lakh as per the latest audited balance sheet, proposes to buy back 20% of its equity capital at ₹40 per share. The Articles of Association authorize buy-back. The Board passed a resolution in March 2025 to proceed. To fund this, the company decided to sell investments worth ₹5,000 lakh, which have a book value of ₹6,000 lakh. It has existing borrowings of ₹9,500 lakh.

The company has not made any default in repayment of term loans, debentures, or dividend payments and has filed all statutory returns under Sections 92, 123, 127, and 129 of the Companies Act, 2013. It had completed its previous buy-back in October 2024.

The Board now seeks to implement the buy-back by July 2025.

On the basis of above solve below mentioned mcqs.
question_html: Can Asteria Ltd. proceed with the buy-back based solely on the Board Resolution?

options.A: Yes, because Board Resolution is always sufficient
options.B: No, it must always be by special resolution in general meeting.
options.C: No, because 20% buy-back exceeds the 10% limit allowed for Board Resolution alone.
options.D: Yes, because the Articles authorize it and 20% is within the 25% limit.

answer_html: Answer: (C) — Section 68(2) permits a Board Resolution alone to authorise a buy-back only up to 10% of paid-up equity capital and free reserves in a financial year; beyond that (up to the overall 25% cap), a special resolution passed in general meeting is required. Asteria's proposed 20% buy-back exceeds the Board-Resolution-alone threshold, so the March 2025 Board Resolution by itself is not sufficient.
topic_text: Buy-back of Securities (1): Board Resolution alone authorises buy-back only up to 10% of paid-up capital plus free reserves; beyond that a special resolution is required

Asteria Ltd., a listed company with equity share capital of ₹6,000 lakh and free reserves of ₹10,000 lakh as per the latest audited balance sheet, proposes to buy back 20% of its equity capital at ₹40 per share. On the basis of above solve below mentioned mcqs.
question_html: What is the maximum permissible buy-back limit for Asteria Ltd. under the Resource Test as per Section?
answer_html: Answer: (A) ₹4,000 lakh — the Resource Test under Section 68(2)(c) caps buy-back at 25% of (paid-up equity capital + free reserves) = 25% × (₹6,000 lakh + ₹10,000 lakh) = 25% × ₹16,000 lakh = ₹4,000 lakh.
topic_text: Buy-back of Securities (1): Resource Test caps buy-back at 25% of paid-up capital plus free reserves

On the basis of above solve below mentioned mcqs.
question_html: After completing the proposed buy-back, will Asteria Ltd. satisfy the Debt-Equity Ratio condition under Section?

options.A: Yes, because total debt is within 2:1 ratio post buy-back
options.B: No, because the loss on investment increases the debt
options.C: No, because buy-back reduces reserves, tightening equity base
options.D: Yes, because CRR creation boosts equity buffer

answer_html: Answer: (A) — Section 68(2)(d) requires post-buy-back debt not to exceed twice (paid-up capital + free reserves). Existing borrowings are ₹9,500 lakh against a pre-buy-back capital+reserves base of ₹16,000 lakh; even after buy-back utilises up to the ₹4,000 lakh Resource-Test ceiling (reducing the base to around ₹12,000 lakh), the resulting ratio (₹9,500 lakh ÷ ₹12,000 lakh ≈ 0.79:1) remains comfortably within the 2:1 statutory limit.
topic_text: Buy-back of Securities (1): Post-buy-back Debt-Equity Ratio test caps total debt at twice paid-up capital plus free reserves

question_html: In the books of G Ltd., closing inventory as at 31.03.2024 amounts to ₹10,40,000 (on the basis of FIFO method). The company decides to change from FIFO method to weighted average method for ascertaining the cost of inventory for 31.3.2024. On the basis of weighted average method, closing inventory as on 31.03.2024 amounts to ₹8,80,000. Realisable value of the inventory as on 31.03.2024 amounts to ₹12,00,000. What will be the value of inventory in the books and what disclosure should be given in the financial statement on 31.3.2024?

options.A: The value of inventory will be ₹8,80,000 and the fact that the valuation method has changed to be disclosed in the financial statement.
options.B: The value of inventory will be ₹12,00,000, and full disclosure with the amount the valuation method has changed to be disclosed in the financial statement.
options.C: The value of inventory will be ₹12,00,000, and the fact that valuation method has changed to be disclosed in the financial statement.
options.D: The value of inventory will be ₹8,80,000, and full disclosure with the amount the valuation method has changed to be disclosed in the financial statement.

answer_html: Answer: (D) — inventory is valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value; under the newly-adopted weighted-average method, cost is ₹8,80,000, which is lower than the ₹12,00,000 NRV, so ₹8,80,000 is the value carried in the books. Because a change in inventory cost formula is a change in accounting policy, AS 1 requires disclosure not merely of the *fact* that the method changed, but also of the *quantified financial effect/amount* of the change — ruling out the lighter-disclosure option (A) with the same value.
topic_text: AS 2 (1.10): Change of cost formula valued at lower of new-method cost and NRV, with full quantified disclosure of the policy change per AS 1

question_html: A Ltd. has a balance of ₹17,15,000 in the loan account with State Finance Corporation which is inclusive of ₹1,15,000 for interest accrued but not due. The loan is secured by hypothecation of the Plant and Machinery. As per Schedule III to the Companies Act, 2013 loan is to be disclosed in the balance sheet as follows:

options.A: Disclosed ₹16,00,000 as a secured loan under long-term borrowings.
options.B: Disclosed ₹16,00,000 as a secured loan under long-term borrowings and ₹1,15,000 under short-term borrowings.
options.C: Disclosed ₹16,00,000 as a secured loan under long-term borrowings and ₹1,15,000 under other current liabilities.
options.D: Disclosed ₹16,00,000 as a secured loan under long-term borrowings and no disclosure for ₹1,15,000.

answer_html: Answer: (C) — the principal loan balance, net of the interest component (₹17,15,000 − ₹1,15,000 = ₹16,00,000), stays under Long-Term Borrowings (secured, hypothecation-backed). Interest accrued but not yet due is not itself a "borrowing" — per Schedule III it is disclosed separately under Other Current Liabilities, not lumped into long-term borrowings and not mislabelled as a short-term borrowing (which would imply it is itself a loan).

case_facts_html:
On 1st April, 2019, Black Limited received a government grant of ₹15,00,000 for acquisition of a Machine costing ₹50,00,000. The grant was credited to the cost of the Machine. The life of the Machine is expected to be 10 years and estimated residual value at the end of 10 years is ₹5,00,000. The company charges depreciation on straight line basis.

Due to non-fulfillment of certain conditions the company had to refund the entire grant on 1st April, 2021.

On 31st March, 2023, Black Limited received certain indications of impairment of the Machine and the recoverable amount was ascertained to be ₹28,00,000 with revised useful life of 4 years and nil residual value.

On 1st April, 2024, the company exchanged the Machine by paying cash of ₹2,00,000 and new Machine valued at ₹18,00,000.

Based on the information given in above Case Scenario, answer the following Question No. 1-4:
question_html: What will be the carrying amount of the Machine as on 31st March, 2021 after charging depreciation for the year?
answer_html: Answer: (D) ₹29,00,000 — the grant was credited to (deducted from) the cost of the Machine per AS 12's Method I, so the depreciable amount is ₹50,00,000 − ₹15,00,000 (grant) − ₹5,00,000 (residual value) = ₹30,00,000 over a 10-year life, i.e. ₹3,00,000 p.a. on the straight-line basis. Carrying amount at 31 March 2021 (two years' depreciation, FY2019-20 and FY2020-21) = ₹35,00,000 − (2 × ₹3,00,000) = ₹29,00,000.
topic_text: AS 12 (1.6): Presentation of grants related to specific fixed assets - Method I, grant deducted from asset's gross value, reducing depreciation

answer_html: Answer: (A) ₹4,87,500 — on refund of a grant related to a specific asset, AS 12 requires the book value of the asset to be increased by the refunded amount, with depreciation on the revised book value provided prospectively over its residual useful life. case_facts_html:
The following particulars are stated in the Balance Sheet of Star Limited as on 31st March, 2023: Deferred Tax Assets (Dr.) ₹1,20,000; Deferred Tax Liabilities (Cr.) ₹2,10,000.

The following transactions were reported during the year 2023-24: (1) Depreciation as per accounting records ₹12,00,000. (2) Depreciation as per income tax records ₹18,00,000. (3) Interest paid accounted in books on accrual basis ₹4,50,000 but paid on 15-05-2024. (4) Employer PF Contribution exp. disallowed for tax purpose ₹82,000 in year 2022-23 but allowed in year 2023-24. (5) Unamortized preliminary expenses as per tax records ₹1,00,000. (6) Donation ₹70,000. (7) Tax Rate 20%.

Based on the information given in above Case Scenario, answer the following Question No. 5-8.
question_html: What would be the value of the Deferred Tax Assets as on 31-03-2024?
answer_html: Answer: (C) ₹1,23,600. Opening DTA ₹1,20,000, less reversal of last year's PF-contribution-disallowance DTA (₹82,000 × 20% = ₹16,400, since the amount disallowed in 2022-23 is now allowed in 2023-24), plus a new DTA on the unamortized preliminary expenses still to be claimed for tax (₹1,00,000 × 20% = ₹20,000). The interest accrued in books but paid on 15-05-2024 creates no timing difference: since it was paid before the due date of filing the return of income, Section 43B's proviso allows it as a deduction in the year of accrual itself, so no DTA arises on this item. Net: ₹1,20,000 − ₹16,400 + ₹20,000 = ₹1,23,600.

topic_text: AS 22 (4.5): Measurement of deferred tax assets - timing differences reversing/originating, and the Sec 43B proviso exception for interest paid before the return-filing due date

question_html: AB Contractors undertakes a fixed price contract of ₹350 Lakhs. Information related to contract is given as under: Material purchased ₹125 lakhs. Labour charges ₹95 lakhs. Unused material ₹22 lakhs. Estimated future costs to be incurred to complete the contract ₹115 Lakhs. Payment received as part payment of contract ₹50 Lakhs. Machinery used for 4 years for the contract. Original cost of the machine is ₹210 Lakhs. Expected life of machinery is 20 years. What will be the Profit/Loss on the contract?
answer_html: Answer: (A) Loss on contract ₹5 lakhs. Cost incurred to date = Material purchased ₹125 lakhs − Unused material ₹22 lakhs (excluded, not yet consumed) + Labour ₹95 lakhs + Depreciation on machinery attributable to the contract (₹210 lakhs ÷ 20 years × 4 years used = ₹42 lakhs) = ₹240 lakhs. Total estimated contract cost = ₹240 lakhs (incurred) + ₹115 lakhs (future cost to complete) = ₹355 lakhs, against a contract price of ₹350 lakhs. Since total estimated cost exceeds the contract price, AS 7 requires the entire foreseeable loss to be recognised immediately: ₹355 lakhs − ₹350 lakhs = ₹5 lakhs loss.
topic_text: AS 7 (1.6): Percentage of Completion Method - immediate recognition of the entire foreseeable loss when total estimated cost exceeds contract price

question_html: Ace Limited borrowed ₹25 Lakhs from ABN Bank during the financial year 2023-24. Ace Limited used these funds to invest in Equity shares of Kay Limited. Kay Limited is implementing a new Project, so with these future prospects, Ace Limited invested ₹25 Lakhs in Kay Limited. As on 31st March, 2024, since the said project was not complete, the directors of Ace Limited capitalised the interest on loan amounting to ₹2 lakhs and thus added the amount of interest to the cost of Investments. Market value of these investments on 31st March, 2024 is ₹24 Lakhs. Identify the correct statement, considering the above facts as per AS 16:

options.A: Interest paid is acquisition charge, hence directors of Ace Limited correctly added the amount of interest in cost of investment.
options.B: Since project is qualifying Asset, directors of Ace Limited correctly added the amount of interest in cost of investments.
options.C: Ace Limited invested in equity share which is not a qualifying asset, therefore directors are wrong to add the interest in cost of investments, rather it should be charged to profit and loss account.
options.D: Since project is qualifying asset, directors of Ace Limited should capitalise the interest amount to market value of investments, rather than cost of investments.

answer_html: Answer: (C) — the qualifying-asset test under AS 16 applies to Ace Limited's own asset, i.e. the investment in equity shares, which is a financial asset and never a "qualifying asset" (an asset that itself necessarily takes a substantial period to get ready for its intended use) regardless of what Kay Limited (the investee) is doing with the funds. Since Ace Limited holds no qualifying asset of its own, none of the borrowing cost may be capitalised; the ₹2 lakh interest must be charged to the Profit and Loss Account.
topic_text: AS 16 (4.5): Recognition criteria - capitalisation restricted to borrowing costs directly attributable to acquisition/construction of a qualifying asset held by the borrowing entity itself

question_html: Glow Limited had taken a loan of ₹5,00,000 in June, 2023. The loan is to be repaid in 10 half yearly equal installments starting from December, 2023. Determine how the remaining loan will be classified in the Balance Sheet as on 31st March, 2024 as per Schedule III of the Companies Act, 2013?

options.A: ₹3,50,000 is to be shown under the head 'Long term borrowings and ₹1,00,000 is to be shown under the head 'Short term borrowings"
options.B: ₹3,50,000 is to be shown under the head 'Long term borrowings and ₹75,000 is to be shown under the head "Short term borrowings" and ₹25,000 is to be shown under the head 'Other Current liabilities."
options.C: ₹4,50,000 is to be shown under the head 'Long term borrowings'
options.D: ₹3,50,000 is to be shown under the head 'Long term borrowings' and ₹1,00,000 is to be shown under the head 'Other Current liabilities.'

answer_html:
Answer: the source's printed Answer Key states (A). Working: instalments of ₹50,000 each fall due Dec 2023, Jun 2024, Dec 2024 ... Jun 2028 (10 total). One instalment (Dec 2023) is paid before the 31 March 2024 balance sheet date, leaving ₹4,50,000 outstanding, of which the Jun 2024 and Dec 2024 instalments (₹1,00,000) fall due within the next 12 months and ₹3,50,000 remains due beyond 12 months.

Flagging an independent-derivation discrepancy: per Note 6(A) to Schedule III's General Instructions for the Balance Sheet, "current maturities of long-term debt" are disclosed as a separate line item under 'Other Current Liabilities', not under 'Short-term borrowings' — which would point to option (D), not (A), for the ₹1,00,000 due within 12 months. This exact classification point ("current-vs-long-term loan classification") is even called out as a worked example in this repo's own AS-index for the Schedule III unit. We are not overriding the source's printed answer letter (A) — it is reproduced verbatim — but flagging this as a possible inconsistency in the source's own key for Pranav's judgment, per the never-silently-fix rule.

answer_html: Answer: (C) ₹7,50,000 — per the exception in AS 16 for foreign-currency borrowings that are, in substance, a hedge against interest cost, the recognised borrowing cost is capped at what the equivalent local-currency borrowing (₹75,00,000 × 10%) would have cost.

case_facts_html:
P Limited took a loan of USD 1,00,000 on 1st April, 2024 for a specific project at 5% p.a., payable annually. Exchange rate 1st April, 2024: ₹75/USD; 31st March, 2025: ₹80/USD. The equivalent amount could have been borrowed locally at 10% p.a.

P Limited holds 12% of the voting shares in G Limited. G Limited's board comprises eight members, two of whom are appointed by P Limited, casting significant influence.

P Limited manufactures toys at Muzaffarnagar: Material Cost ₹200/unit, Direct Labour ₹40/unit, Direct Variable Production Overheads ₹20/unit. Plant capacity 1,00,000 units p.a.; fixed production overheads ₹15,00,000 p.a. Actual production 2024-25: 1,20,000 units. 11,000 units of finished toys unsold at year end.

P Limited also renders catering services. At a 2024-25 wedding it catered, ten people died possibly from food poisoning. Legal proceedings seek ₹10,00,000 compensation; P Limited disputes liability. Legal counsel advises the company is likely to lose, though chances of paying the claim are not remote. Estimated: (i) legal cost ₹75,000 (irrespective of outcome); (ii) settlement if claim paid ₹10,00,000.

Based on the information given above, answer Question Nos. 1–5.
question_html: What is the relationship of G Limited with P Limited as per the relevant Accounting Standard?

options.A: G Limited is a subsidiary of P Limited.
options.B: G Limited is an associate of P Limited.
options.C: G Limited is a Joint Venture of P Limited.
options.D: P Limited has invested in G Limited with no further relationship as subsidiary, associate or joint venture.

answer_html: Answer: (B) Associate — despite holding only 12% of voting shares, P Limited has significant influence via board representation (2 of 8 board seats), which AS 23 treats as evidence of significant influence independent of the 20% voting-power presumption.

Deferred tax information as at 31st March, 2025: Depreciation per accounting records ₹4,00,000; Depreciation allowable under Section 32 of the Income Tax Act ₹10,00,000; Unamortized Preliminary Expenses per tax records ₹30,000; GST penalty imposed 30th March, 2025, payable 30th April, 2025, ₹1,25,000.

question_html: What amount should be recognized by V Limited as Revenue and Total Expenses in respect of the hostel building contract in its Statement of Profit and Loss for the year ended 31st March, 2025 as per provisions of Accounting Standard 7 (Revised)?

options.A: Revenue of 84 lakhs, Total Expense of ₹60 lakhs.

question_html: What would be the carrying amount of Investment in M Limited in the Consolidated Financial Statements of V Limited as at 31st March, 2025?
answer_html: Answer: (B) ₹26,00,000 — under the equity method: cost ₹20,00,000, plus V Limited's 30% share of M Limited's post-acquisition-period profit (M's FY2024-25 profit of ₹30,00,000 accrues evenly over the year; V held the investment for 10 of the 12 months, 1st June 2024 to 31st March 2025, so the relevant share is ₹30,00,000 × 10/12 × 30% = ₹7,50,000), less the dividend received during the holding period (the ₹5,00,000 dividend declared 14th August 2024, of which V's 30% share = ₹1,50,000). Total: ₹20,00,000 + ₹7,50,000 − ₹1,50,000 = ₹26,00,000. The dividend reduces the carrying amount either way under the equity method — unlike the cost method, whether it was declared out of pre- or post-acquisition profit does not change this: the equity method already picks up the investor's share of the investee's profit as it is earned, so a dividend received is simply a cash realisation of value already reflected in the carrying amount, and always reduces it. (The later 15th June 2025 dividend is after the balance sheet date and irrelevant here.)

topic_text: AS 23 (2.6): Equity method - carrying amount adjusted for investor's share of post-acquisition profit (time-apportioned) and always reduced by dividends received, regardless of pre/post-acquisition profit source

question_html: PQR Ltd. sold machinery worth ₹2 crores to its subsidiary STU Pvt. Ltd. at arm's length price, paid ₹50 lakhs remuneration to its CEO/CFO, and received a ₹1 crore loan from its holding company LMN Ltd. All disclosed separately in notes to accounts. Which statement correctly reflects the application of AS 18 in this scenario?

options.A: AS 18 does not apply to transactions with subsidiaries.
options.B: Remuneration paid to CEO and CFO need not be disclosed under AS 18.
options.C: AS 18 requires disclosure of related party transactions such as sale of machinery, loans, and managerial remuneration.

case_facts_html:
Gray Ltd. is engaged in the business of constructing towers since 15 years. Alpha Ltd gave a contract to Gray Ltd. for construction of 2 towers.

Contract price for 2 towers is agreed at ₹160 crore. (each tower has contract price of ₹80 crore)

At the time of contract, Gray Ltd has estimated that the contract cost will be ₹141 crore. It is assumed that construction will be completed in 3 years.

At the end of year 1, Gray Ltd has revised the construction cost to ₹150 crore.

At the beginning of year 2, the customer has requested for a variation in the contract. Customer now wants construction of 3 towers instead of 2 towers. The term of the contract will not change, construction of all the towers will be completed simultaneously.

As a result of this variation, contract price will increase by ₹80 crore and contract costs will increase by ₹75 crore.

Gray Ltd has decided to measure the stage of completion on the basis of the proportion of contract costs incurred to the total estimated contract costs.

Contract costs incurred at the end of each year is: Year 1: ₹35.25 crore. Year 2: ₹148.5 crore (including unused material of ₹2.25 crore) Year 3: Total Revised contract costs.

Based on the information given in above Case Scenario, answer the following Question 1 - 3.
question_html: What is the stage of completion of contract on the basis of proportion of contract costs incurred to the total estimated contract costs at the end of year 1 and Year 2 respectively?
answer_html: Answer: (B) Year 1: 23.5% and Year 2: 65% — Year 1 stage of completion = costs incurred to date (₹35.25 crore) ÷ the revised total estimated cost available at that date (₹150 crore) = 23.5%. Year 2 stage of completion uses the cost incurred net of the unused material not yet consumed on site (₹148.5 crore − ₹2.25 crore = ₹146.25 crore, since AS 7 excludes costs relating to future contract activity when measuring stage of completion, even though the material remains part of total costs incurred) divided by the revised total contract cost for all 3 towers (₹150 crore + ₹75 crore for the added tower = ₹225 crore): ₹146.25 crore ÷ ₹225 crore = 65%.
topic_text: AS 7 (1.9): Stage of completion under the cost-proportion method, excluding costs relating to future activity (e.g. unused material) from the numerator
