options.D: Year 1: ₹37.60 crore, Year 2: ₹120.80 crore and Year 3: ₹81.60 crore

answer_html: Answer: (C) Year 1: ₹37.60 crore, Year 2: ₹118.40 crore, Year 3: ₹84 crore. Year 1 revenue = 23.5% × ₹160 crore (original 2-tower price) = ₹37.60 crore. From Year 2, the contract price is revised for the added tower to ₹240 crore (₹160 crore + ₹80 crore); cumulative revenue at 65% stage of completion = ₹240 crore × 65% = ₹156 crore, so Year 2 revenue = ₹156 crore − ₹37.60 crore = ₹118.40 crore. Year 3 (contract completion) revenue = total contract price − cumulative revenue already recognised = ₹240 crore − ₹156 crore = ₹84 crore.
topic_text: AS 7 (1.6): Cumulative revenue recognition across years, updating the total contract price for a customer-requested variation

question_html: X Ltd. has entered into a binding agreement with Beta Ltd. to buy a custom-made machine for ₹2 lakhs. During the year 2024-25 X Ltd has to change its method of production due to changes in market trend. Before the delivery of the machine, X Ltd had already changed its method of production and the new method will not require the machine ordered. Now the company decides to scrap it after delivery. The expected scrap value is ₹25,000. Machine was received on 10th October, 2024 and was scrapped on 15th October, 2024. The correct accounting treatment for above machine in the year 2024-25 is -

options.A: Machine A/c to be debited with ₹2 lakhs and Bank A/c to be credited with ₹2 lakhs.
options.B: Impairment A/c to be debited with ₹1.75 lakhs and Bank A/c to be credited with ₹1.75 lakhs.
options.C: Profit and Loss A/c to be debited with ₹2 lakhs and Bank A/c to be credited with ₹2 lakhs.
options.D: Profit and Loss A/c to be debited with ₹1.75 lakhs and Bank A/c to be credited with ₹1.75 lakhs.

answer_html: Answer: (D) P&L A/c debited with ₹1.75 lakhs, Bank A/c credited with ₹1.75 lakhs. Since X Ltd already knew, before the machine was even delivered, that it would never be used for its intended purpose, the machine provides no probable future economic benefit and therefore fails AS 10's recognition criteria for Property, Plant and Equipment — it is never capitalised as Machine A/c. The net cost actually borne by the company (₹2,00,000 acquisition cost less ₹25,000 realisable scrap value = ₹1,75,000) is recognised as a loss directly in the Profit and Loss Account.
topic_text: AS 10 (2.5): Recognition criteria - an asset known in advance to provide no future economic benefit is never capitalised as PPE

question_html: ABC Ltd. is in the business of creating contents for various OTT platforms. The company has developed a technical know-how (the asset) by incurring expenditure of ₹25 lakhs. The company started using the asset from 1st April 2019. The management of the company is of the view that the asset has infinite lifetime and therefore has not amortized the asset till date. What should be the total amortization amount (including current as well as the previous years amortization) to be charged to Profit and loss account for the year ended March 31st 2024, with reference to AS 26?

options.A: Nil, as per the management the know how has infinite life and the management is correct.
options.B: ₹25 lakhs as the know how is an intangible asset as per AS 26.
options.C: ₹12.5 lakhs (including current year's amortization of ₹2.5 lakhs) to be charged to Profit and loss Account.
options.D: ₹15 lakhs (including current year's amortization of ₹2.5 lakhs) to be charged to Profit and Loss account.

answer_html: Answer: (C) ₹12.5 lakhs (including current year's amortisation of ₹2.5 lakhs). AS 26 does not accept "infinite life" for an intangible asset — it carries a rebuttable presumption that useful life cannot exceed ten years from the date the asset is available for use, unless there is persuasive evidence of a longer (still finite) life, which management has not demonstrated here. Amortisable amount = ₹25 lakhs over the maximum 10-year period = ₹2.5 lakhs per year. From 1st April 2019 to 31st March 2024 is 5 complete years (2019-20 through 2023-24), so cumulative amortisation to be caught up and charged = 5 × ₹2.5 lakhs = ₹12.5 lakhs, which includes the current year's ₹2.5 lakhs.
topic_text: AS 26 (6.19-6.23): Rebuttable presumption that an intangible asset's useful life cannot exceed ten years from the date it becomes available for use

case_facts_html:
Health India Limited (HIL), incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013, is engaged in the production and distribution of medicines. It has manufacturing plants at Baddi (Himachal Pradesh) and Bhopal (Madhya Pradesh). It also imports medicines from Pharma Inc. New York (United States).

On 1st Jan 2024, HIL sold 2,00,000 strips of Medicine to Dee Limited for ₹50 Lakhs on 60 days of credit. Cost per strip of this medicine, was ₹20. (i.e.) total cost ₹40 Lakhs (2,00,000 strips@₹20). Dee Ltd. paid 20% of the amount due on 5th January, 2024. In March 2024, Dee Limited is having significant cash flow issues and is trying to raise funds through bank loan to run its operations. However, it is unable to do so and not able to release payment to HIL on due date. Subsequent to this, it has gone under liquidation on 15th March, 2024. At the time when medicine was sold by HIL to Dee Limited, there was no reason for HIL to believe that it will not be able to collect the sales proceeds from Dee Limited in future.

On 1st April, 2023 HIL has made an investment of ₹200 Lakhs in the equity shares of Rose Limited of which 50% is made in the long-term category i.e. long-term investment and rest as temporary investment i.e. current investment. The realisable value of all such investments on 31st March, 2024 becomes ₹50 Lakhs as Rose Limited lost a copyright. From the given market conditions, it is apparent that the reduction in the value of investment is not temporary in nature.

HIL imported medicine from Pharma Inc. for a sum. of US $ 2,50,000 on 1st January, 2024. HIL released full payment on 17th April, 2024 to Medicine Ltd. The exchange rates are as follows:

Exchange rate per $
1st April, 2023₹76
1st January, 2024₹81
31st March, 2024₹80
17th April, 2024₹79

HIL is working on a strategic plan to close the production unit of Bhopal due to change in technology. The board of directors approved the closure of Bhopal Plan on 1st March, 2024. The company did a formal announcement regarding closure to the affected parties on 10th March, 2024. The company entered into a binding-sale agreement on 21 April, 2024.

Reporting date of the company is 31st March, 2024.

Based on the information given in the above Case Scenario, answer the following Question No. 6 to 9.
question_html: How the recognition of revenue from sales of medicine to Dee Limited will be done by HIL under AS 9 and what would be the treatment of unrealized amount for the year ended 31st March, 2024?

options.A: Revenue will be recognised for ₹50 Lakhs, subsequently unrealized amount ₹50 lakhs will be debited to bad debts A/c.
options.B: Revenue will be recognised for ₹40 Lakhs, subsequently unrealized amount ₹40 lakhs will be debited to bad debts A/c.
options.C: Revenue will be recognised for ₹50 Lakhs, subsequently unrealized amount ₹40 lakhs will be debited to bad debts A/c.
options.D: Revenue will be recognised for ₹40 Lakhs, unrealised amount of ₹40 lakhs will be shown in Sundry Debtors list.

answer_html: Answer: (C) Revenue recognised for ₹50 Lakhs, subsequently unrealised amount ₹40 lakhs debited to bad debts A/c. At the point of sale (1st January, 2024), HIL had no reason to doubt Dee Limited's ability to pay, so the full ₹50 lakh sale value is recognised as revenue under AS 9. Dee Ltd. paid 20% (₹10 lakhs) on 5th January, 2024; the remaining ₹40 lakhs became uncollectable once Dee Limited went into liquidation, and this post-sale uncertainty is accounted for as a bad debt (a separate subsequent event), not as a reversal of revenue already recognised.
topic_text: AS 9 (2.9): Revenue recognised in full where no uncertainty existed at the time of sale; a later inability to collect is a separate bad-debts event, not a revenue adjustment

question_html: How will you recognize the reduction in the value of the investments in the financial statements for the year ended 31st March 2024 as per AS 13 (Revised)?

options.A: The reduction of ₹50 Lakhs in the carrying value of current investment will be charged to the profit and loss account. There will be no impact on the value of long-term investments.
options.B: The reduction of ₹75 Lakhs in the carrying value of current investment will be charged to the profit and loss account. There will be no impact on the value of long-term investments.
options.C: The reduction of ₹75 Lakhs in the carrying value of current investment will be charged to the profit and loss account. The reduction of ₹75 Lakhs in the carrying value of long-term investment will also be charged to the profit and loss account.
options.D: The reduction of ₹75 Lakhs in the carrying value of current investment will be charged to the profit and loss account. The reduction of ₹75 Lakhs in the carrying value of long-term investment will also be charged to capital reserve account.

Current investments are always carried at the lower of cost and fair value, so the ₹75 lakh fall goes to P&L. Because the fall in the long-term investment is explicitly stated to be "other than temporary" in nature, AS 13 requires that decline to also be charged to the Profit and Loss Account — a capital reserve credit/debit is not the mechanism AS 13 uses for investment write-downs.
topic_text: AS 13 (3.6): Current investments carried at lower of cost and fair value; an other-than-temporary decline in a long-term investment is also charged to the profit and loss account

question_html: Ascertain the loss/gain due to change in foreign exchange rates to be recognised in the financial statements for the year ended 31st March, 2024 as per AS 11.

options.A: ₹2,50,000 Exchange gain should be credited to profit and loss account.

question_html: What would be the date of "initial disclosure of event" be considered for Bhopal Plant?

question_html: X Ltd. sold Plant & Machinery having WDV of ₹60 lakhs to Y Ltd. for ₹75 lakhs (Fair value of ₹75 Lakhs) and the same plant was leased back by Y Ltd. to X Ltd. The lease back is in the nature of operating lease. The treatment will be:

options.A: X Ltd. should amortize the profit of ₹15 lakhs over the lease term.
options.B: X Ltd. should recognize the Profit of ₹15 lakhs immediately.
options.C: No profit/loss, as fair value is equal to sale price.
options.D: Y Ltd. should recognize the profit of ₹15 lakhs immediately.

answer_html: Answer: (B) X Ltd. (the seller-lessee) should recognise the profit of ₹15 lakhs (₹75 lakhs sale price − ₹60 lakhs WDV) immediately. Under AS 19's sale-and-leaseback rules for an operating lease-back, when the sale price is equal to the fair value of the asset, the transaction is treated as a normal sale and any resulting profit or loss is recognised immediately by the seller-lessee, with no deferral over the lease term (deferral applies only to a finance lease-back, or to specific fair-value-mismatch cases under an operating lease-back).
topic_text: AS 19 (5.10): Sale and leaseback as an operating lease where sale price equals fair value - profit recognised immediately by the seller-lessee

On 1st April, 2024 Z Ltd redeemed all its preference shares at a premium of 5%. Z Ltd. bought back 8,00,000 equity shares @ ₹20 per share.

Buy back is fully authorized by Z Ltd.'s articles and necessary resolution has been passed for this. The payment for buy back of shares will be made through available balance in bank account.

To finance Redemption of preference shares and buy back of shares, company has decided to sell its investments for ₹98 Lakhs.

Z Ltd had 80,000 Equity stock options outstanding on the above mentioned date, to the employees @ ₹15 per share when the market price was ₹20 per share. (This was included under the head current liabilities). On 1st April, 2024, 70% of the employees exercised their options.

question_html: What will be the balance of capital redemption reserve as on 31st March 2025?
answer_html: Answer: (B) ₹330 Lakhs. Opening CRR = ₹50 lakhs. Preference shares (₹200 lakhs nominal) were redeemed wholly out of profits (no fresh issue of shares was made for the specific purpose of the redemption — the ESOP exercise is a separate, unrelated transaction), so a sum equal to the full nominal value, ₹200 lakhs, must be transferred to CRR. The equity buy-back (8,00,000 shares × ₹10 face value = ₹80 lakhs) was funded out of the bank balance (free reserves), so a further ₹80 lakhs must be transferred to CRR. Total CRR = ₹50 lakhs + ₹200 lakhs + ₹80 lakhs = ₹330 lakhs.
topic_text: Buy-back of Securities (1): Capital Redemption Reserve funded from free reserves equal to the nominal value of preference shares redeemed and equity shares bought back

question_html: What will be the Balance of Reserves as on 31st March 2025 excluding capital redemption Reserve?

options.A: General Reserve and Profit Loss ₹323 Lakhs and securities Premium ₹10 lakhs
options.B: General Reserve and Profit Loss ₹243 Lakhs and securities Premium ₹10 lakhs
options.C: General Reserve and Profit Loss ₹323 Lakhs and securities Premium ₹15.60 lakhs
options.D: General Reserve and Profit Loss ₹243 Lakhs and securities Premium ₹15.60 lakhs

answer_html: Answer: (C) General Reserve and Profit & Loss ₹323 lakhs; Securities Premium ₹15.60 lakhs. Securities Premium: opening ₹100 lakhs, less ₹10 lakhs premium on preference redemption, less ₹80 lakhs premium on equity buy-back (8,00,000 shares × ₹10 premium per share, absorbed against Securities Premium since a sufficient balance remained), plus ₹5.60 lakhs premium arising on the ESOP exercise (56,000 shares issued at ₹10 face value against total consideration of ₹8.40 lakhs cash received plus ₹2.80 lakhs reclassified from the Stock Options Outstanding balance for the exercised options, i.e. ₹11.20 lakhs total less ₹5.60 lakhs face value = ₹5.60 lakhs premium): ₹100 − ₹10 − ₹80 + ₹5.60 = ₹15.60 lakhs. question_html: Past Ltd. had the following items under the head "Reserves and Surplus" the Balance Sheet as on 31st March 2025: (Amount ₹ in lakhs) Securities Premium Account 90; Capital Reserve 40; Revaluation Reserve 70. The company had an accumulated loss of ₹280 lakhs on the same date, which was disclosed under the head "Statement of Profit and Loss" as asset in Balance Sheet. What should be disclosed on the face of Balance Sheet as per Schedule III to the Companies Act, 2013?

options.A: Reserve and Surplus-Securities premium 90 lakhs; others ₹110 lakh and Accumulated loss ₹280 lakhs in the Asset side.
options.B: Reserve and Surplus ₹200 lakhs; and Accumulated loss ₹280 lakhs in the Asset side.

answer_html: Answer: (D) Reserve and Surplus − ₹80 lakhs only. Schedule III does not permit an accumulated loss (a debit balance in the Statement of Profit and Loss) to be shown as an asset. It must instead be netted directly within the "Reserves and Surplus" line on the equity side: total credit-balance reserves (₹90 + ₹40 + ₹70 = ₹200 lakhs) less the accumulated loss (₹280 lakhs) = a net negative ₹80 lakhs, disclosed as "Reserves and Surplus − ₹80 lakhs" (a negative figure within Reserves and Surplus, not a positive asset-side item).
topic_text: Preparation of Financial Statements (1.5): An accumulated loss exceeding available reserves is netted within Reserves and Surplus as a negative balance, never shown as an asset

question_html: During the process of Internal Reconstruction, JAY Ltd has come across the following adjustment: There is a contingent liability for which no provision had been made. This contingent liability was settled at ₹7,500 and also ₹6,000 was recovered from the insurance company in this regard. Which of the following is the correct treatment for the above adjustment?

options.A: Reconstruction A/c Dr ₹1,500 and Bank A/c Cr ₹1,500
options.B: Reconstruction A/c Dr ₹7,500 and Bank A/c Cr ₹7,500
options.C: Contingent Liability A/c Dr ₹1,500 and Bank A/c Cr ₹1,500
options.D: Profit and Loss A/c Dr ₹1,500 and Bank A/c Cr ₹1,500

answer_html: Answer: (A) Reconstruction A/c Dr ₹1,500 and Bank A/c Cr ₹1,500. Since this was a previously unprovided contingent liability that crystallised and was settled during the reconstruction scheme, the net cost actually borne by the company (₹7,500 settled − ₹6,000 recovered from insurance = ₹1,500) is the amount debited to the Reconstruction Account, against a credit to Bank A/c for the same net cash outflow.
topic_text: Internal Reconstruction (3): A previously unprovided contingent liability crystallising during reconstruction is debited to the Reconstruction Account net of any related recovery

case_facts_html:
Unicorn Limited manufactures building material. It took a loan of ₹60 Lakhs @10% p.a. on 1st August, 2025 to purchase raw material, and on the same day purchased 40,000 units of raw material @ ₹125 per unit (2 units of raw material per unit of finished goods). On 31st March, 2026: (i) 10,000 units of finished goods produced; (ii) NRV of finished goods ₹300/unit; (iii) Net replacement value of raw material ₹100/unit; (iv) Labour and variable overheads ₹10,00,000 for 10,000 units; (v) all finished goods produced remained in stock; (vi) no opening stock of raw material or finished goods.

Unicorn Limited used 15,000 units of raw material to construct an asset (Qualifying Asset). Labour and other overhead charges for construction ₹9,00,000. Paid ₹1,50,000 to install the asset at factory premises.

Unicorn Limited used the balance loan proceeds of ₹10,00,000 to invest in Equity shares of Royal Limited: 90,000 equity shares (Face value ₹10 each) for ₹10,00,000 on 25th March, 2026. Royal Limited declared and paid dividend @20% on 30th March 2026 for the year 2024-25.

A fraud of ₹2,80,000 done by the cashier of Unicorn Limited in January, 2026 was detected in April, 2026. The financial statements for the year ended 31st March, 2026 were approved by the Board of Directors on 1st May, 2026.

Based on the information given in the above case scenario, answer Question Nos. 6–9.
question_html: What would be the value of closing stock of Raw Material and Finished goods as on 31st March, 2026?

options.A: Closing Stock of Raw Material ₹5,00,000 and Finished goods ₹35,00,000.
options.B: Closing Stock of Raw Material ₹5,00,000 and Finished goods ₹30,00,000.
options.C: Closing Stock of Raw Material ₹6,25,000 and Finished goods ₹30,00,000.
options.D: Closing Stock of Raw Material ₹6,25,000 and Finished goods ₹35,00,000.

answer_html: Answer: (B) — finished-goods cost per unit is ₹350 (₹250 material [2 units RM × ₹125] + ₹100 labour/variable overhead), against an NRV of ₹300/unit — since FG cost exceeds NRV, the finished goods are expected to sell below cost, which under AS 2 is precisely the condition that requires the raw material feeding them to be written down to its replacement cost of ₹100/unit rather than kept at the original ₹125/unit. Closing RM: 5,000 units (40,000 purchased − 15,000 used for the qualifying asset − 20,000 consumed in the 10,000 finished units) × ₹100 = ₹5,00,000. Closing FG: 10,000 units at the lower of cost (₹350) and NRV (₹300) = ₹300 × 10,000 = ₹30,00,000.
topic_text: AS 2 (1.14): Materials held for use in production are written down to replacement cost when the finished product they produce is expected to sell below cost

question_html: Volt Tech Limited manufactures electric Vehicle (EV) batteries. The accountant showed Profit Before Tax (PBT) of ₹14,00,000 for the third quarter ending 31st December, 2025 after incorporating: (i) sales promotion expenses of ₹50,000 during the quarter, 80% deferred to the fourth quarter as sales in last quarter is high; (ii) gain on sale of investments in the first quarter of ₹1,60,000, apportioned equally to the four quarters; (iii) additional depreciation of ₹80,000 from a change in depreciation method, entirely debited in the third quarter though the third quarter's own share is only ₹20,000. What amount should be reported as adjusted Profit Before Tax for third quarter?
answer_html: Answer: (A) ₹13,20,000, from ₹14,00,000 reported − ₹80,000 net correction: (i) −₹40,000 — sales promotion expense does not meet the definition of an asset at an interim date, so AS 25 does not allow deferring 80% of it to Q4 merely because Q4's sales are expected to be higher; the full ₹50,000 must be expensed in Q3, so the ₹40,000 the accountant deferred is expensed now. (ii) −₹40,000 — a one-time gain on sale of investments should not be anticipated or spread across quarters (AS 25 treats such occasional gains the same way as seasonal/occasional revenue — recognised when they arise), so the ₹40,000 apportioned to Q3 is reversed; the full ₹1,60,000 belongs in Q1. (iii) Nil adjustment — the cumulative effect of a mid-year change in depreciation method is recognised entirely in the quarter of change, not spread over the remaining quarters, so the full ₹80,000 correctly stays in Q3 as reported; the stated "₹20,000 own share" is the distractor here, not something to adjust for.
topic_text: AS 25 (7.10/7.11/7.12): Costs not meeting the asset definition are expensed as incurred, not deferred to match anticipated future revenue; one-time gains are not apportioned across quarters; a mid-year accounting-estimate change is recognised in full in the period of change

case_facts_html:
Mr. Vikram took a loan of ₹6,00,000 carrying interest @ 10% p.a. on 1st August, 2023 to purchase raw material. He purchased 4000 units of raw material @ ₹125 per unit. Replacement cost of raw material as on 31 March, 2024 is ₹100 per unit. Labour charges and variable overheads incurred are ₹1,00,000 to produce 1000 units of finished goods.

1000 units of Finished goods are produced with raw material (for every unit of finished goods produced, 2 units of raw material are required). Net realizable value of finished good is ₹300 per unit. All the finished goods produced are lying in stock as on 31 March, 2024.

There is no opening stock of raw material and finished goods.

Mr. Vikram used 1500 units of raw material to construct an Asset (Qualifying Asset). Labour and other overhead charges incurred on construction of asset are ₹90,000. Mr. Vikram also paid ₹15,000 to install the asset at Factory premises. Mr. Vikram used Balance of loan proceeds of ₹1,00,000 to invest in Equity Shares of P. Ltd. He purchased 9,000 Equity shares (Face Value ₹10 each) for ₹1,00,000 on 25th March, 2024.

The P. Ltd declared and paid dividend @ 20% on 30th March for the year 2023-24.

Based on the information given in above Case Scenario, answer the following Question No. 1-4:
question_html: What would be the value of closing stock of Raw Material X and Finished Goods as on 31st March 2024?

options.A: Closing Stock of Raw Material X ₹50,000 and closing stock of Finished Goods ₹3,50,000
options.B: Closing Stock of Raw Material X ₹50,000 and closing stock of Finished Goods ₹3,00,000
options.C: Closing Stock of Raw Material X ₹62,500 and closing stock of Finished Goods ₹3,50,000
options.D: Closing Stock of Raw Material X ₹62,500 and closing stock of Finished Goods ₹3,00,000

answer_html: Answer: (B) Closing Stock of Raw Material X ₹50,000 and closing stock of Finished Goods ₹3,00,000 — of the 4,000 units of raw material purchased, 2,000 units went into the 1,000 finished-goods units and 1,500 units into the self-constructed asset, leaving 500 units as closing raw-material stock. Finished-goods cost = (2,000 units × ₹125 material) + ₹1,00,000 labour/overheads = ₹3,50,000 for 1,000 units, i.e. ₹350/unit, against an NRV of only ₹300/unit — since the finished goods will be sold below cost, AS 2's rule that "materials are not written down below cost if the finished products they will be incorporated into are expected to be sold at or above cost" no longer protects the raw material: it must instead be written down to its replacement cost of ₹100/unit as the best available measure of its NRV. Closing Raw Material = 500 × ₹100 = ₹50,000. Closing Finished Goods = 1,000 × lower of cost (₹350) and NRV (₹300) = 1,000 × ₹300 = ₹3,00,000.
topic_text: AS 2 (1.14): NRV of materials held for use - written down to replacement cost once the finished product they'll be incorporated into is expected to sell below cost

question_html: As per AS 16 what will be the amount of interest to be capitalized and amount of interest to be charged to Profit & Loss A/c?

options.A: ₹12,500 interest to be capitalised and ₹27,500 interest to be charged to Profit & Loss A/c
options.B: ₹12,500 interest to be capitalised and ₹20,833 interest to be charged to Profit & Loss A/c
options.C: ₹19,167 interest to be capitalised and ₹20,833 interest to be charged to Profit & Loss A/c

answer_html: Answer: (A) ₹12,500 capitalised, ₹27,500 charged to P&L — total interest on the ₹6,00,000 loan for 1 Aug 2023 to 31 Mar 2024 (8 months) = ₹6,00,000 × 10% × 8/12 = ₹40,000. Of the ₹6,00,000 loan, ₹1,87,500 (the 1,500 units of raw material, at ₹125/unit, used to build the qualifying asset) financed the qualifying asset; the remaining ₹4,12,500 (2,000 units for finished goods + 500 units unused stock + the ₹1,00,000 share investment) did not. case_facts_html:
Kay Ltd. sold goods of ₹22,00,000 to Mr. Ravi Kumar on 1st February, 2024 but at the request of the buyer, these goods were delivered on 10th April 2024.

Kay Ltd. also sold ₹2,00,000 goods on approval basis on 1st January, 2024 to Sheetal Enterprises. The period of approval is 3 months after which they were considered sold. Buyer sent disapproval for 25% of goods and approval for 50% of goods till 31 March, 2024.

Mr. Ravi Kumar has commenced legal action against Kay Ltd. for supply of faulty goods to claim damages. The lawyers of Kay Ltd. have advised that it is not remote yet that resources may be required to settle the claim. Legal cost to be incurred irrespective of the outcome of the case is ₹45,000. Settlement amount if the claim is required to be paid ₹5,00,000.

Sheetal Enterprises, a trade receivable of Kay Ltd. suffered a heavy loss due to an earthquake that occurred on 30th March, 2024. The loss was not covered by any insurance policy. In April, 2024, Sheetal Enterprises became bankrupt. The Balance due from Sheetal Enterprises as on 31 March, 2024 is ₹75,000.

Kay Ltd. makes provision for doubtful debts @ 5%.

Based on the information given in above Case Scenario, answer the following Question No. 5-7
question_html: What is the amount to be recognized as Revenue as per AS 9 in the books of Kay Ltd. as on 31 March, 2024?
answer_html: Answer: (A) ₹23,50,000 — the sale to Mr. Ravi Kumar (₹22,00,000) qualifies as a "bill and hold" sale: delivery was deferred only at the buyer's own request, the goods were identified and ready for delivery, so revenue is recognised in full despite the delayed handover. On the approval sale to Sheetal Enterprises (₹2,00,000), the 3-month approval period runs from 1st January to 31st March, i.e. it has elapsed by the year end: the 50% (₹1,00,000) explicitly approved is revenue, the 25% (₹50,000) explicitly disapproved is not, and per AS 9 the remaining 25% (₹50,000) on which the buyer never responded is also recognised as revenue because the time period allowed for rejection has expired without rejection. Total revenue = ₹22,00,000 + ₹1,00,000 + ₹50,000 = ₹23,50,000.
topic_text: AS 9 (2.8): Bill-and-hold sale at buyer's request, and sale-on-approval revenue on formal acceptance or expiry of the rejection period

question_html: P Ltd. has 60% voting right in Q Ltd. Q Ltd. has 20% voting right in R Ltd. Also, P Ltd. directly enjoys voting right of 14% in R Ltd. R Ltd. is a Listed Company and regularly supplies goods to P Ltd. The Management of R Ltd. has not disclosed its relationship with P Ltd. While preparing Financial Statements of P Ltd., which entities would you disclose as related parties with reference to AS-18?

options.D: Neither of Q Ltd. or R Ltd.

answer_html: Answer: (C) Q Ltd. and R Ltd. — P Ltd. holds 60% of Q Ltd., making Q Ltd. a subsidiary and hence a related party by control. Since P Ltd. controls Q Ltd., Q Ltd.'s 20% voting power in R Ltd. is aggregated with P Ltd.'s own direct 14% holding: 20% + 14% = 34% combined voting power in R Ltd., well above the 20% threshold that gives rise to significant influence, making R Ltd. a related party too. R Ltd.'s own management not having disclosed the relationship does not change P Ltd.'s disclosure obligation, since AS 18 places the disclosure duty on the reporting enterprise regardless of the counterparty's conduct.
topic_text: AS 18 (4.3): Aggregating direct and subsidiary-held voting power to test for control/significant influence over a related party

question_html: A Machinery was given on 3 years lease by a dealer of the machinery for equal annual lease rentals to yield 20% profit margin on cost of the machinery, which is Rs. 3,00,000. Economic life of the machinery is 5 years, and estimated output from the machinery in 5 years is as follows: Year I 50,000 units; Year II 60,000 units; Year III 40,000 units; Year IV 65,000 units; Year V 85,000 units. Compute Annual Lease Rent.
answer_html: Answer: (B) ₹60,000 — as a dealer/manufacturer lessor, the fair value (normal selling price) built into the lease is cost plus the stated profit margin: ₹3,00,000 × 1.20 = ₹3,60,000. The 3-year lease covers only part of the machine's 5-year economic life, so only the portion of that value corresponding to the output actually consumed during the lease term is recoverable through rent: output in Years 1-3 (50,000+60,000+40,000 = 1,50,000 units) is exactly half of the machine's total 5-year output (50,000+60,000+40,000+65,000+85,000 = 3,00,000 units). Value to be recovered over the 3-year lease = 50% × ₹3,60,000 = ₹1,80,000, and equal annual rentals = ₹1,80,000 / 3 = ₹60,000.
topic_text: AS 19 (5.8): Manufacturer/dealer lessor selling profit; lease rental recovery apportioned by output consumed during a lease term shorter than total economic life

case_facts_html: PTU Limited has 6 segments: P, Q, R, S, T & U. (₹ in Lakh): External Sales — P 66, Q 94, R 6, S 5, T 70, U 9 (Total 250). Internal Sales — P 10, Q 5, R 10, S 10, T 10, U 5 (Total 50). Result (P&L) — P 22, Q 4, R (4), S 3, T 20, U 1 (Total 46). Total Assets — P 112, Q 147, R 28, S 28, T 21, U 14 (Total 350). Answer Question Nos. 1–4 as per AS 17 'Segment Reporting'.
question_html: Which would be the Reportable Segment on the basis of Revenue Test?
answer_html: Answer: (B) P, Q & T. Total revenue (external+internal) = 300. 10% threshold = 30. P: 66+10=76; Q: 94+5=99; R: 6+10=16; S: 5+10=15; T: 70+10=80; U: 9+5=14. Only P, Q, and T exceed 30.
topic_text: AS 17 (3.3): Revenue reportability test - 10% of total (external+internal) segment revenue

case_facts_html: On 3rd April 2022, ZYX Limited received a State Government grant of ₹150 lakhs for setting up a Manufacturing Unit in a notified backward area. A bank loan of ₹50 lakhs was also obtained on 1st April 2024. Utilisation: Factory building 100.00 (60 grant, 30 loan, remaining 10 unfunded/other); Machinery 50.00 (40 grant, 20 loan — figures as printed, totals per source); Advance for loading vehicle 30.00 (30 grant); Working capital 20.00 (20 grant). Construction and machinery installation completed 31.03.2025; loading vehicle not delivered. Total interest charged by bank for the year 31.03.2025: ₹5,50,000. The grant was credited to a Deferred Grant Account. ₹30 lakhs of the grant (used for machinery) was refunded in March 2025 due to non-compliance. Estimated machinery life 4 years, nil residual value. During 2024-25, the company also received a ₹8 lakh Central Government subsidy for setting up a unit in a notified backward area, in the nature of promoters' contribution. During 2024-25, the company incurred ₹18 lakhs on publicity and research for a new consumer product, marketed the same year but a failure. Answer Question Nos. 5–8.
question_html: What is the amount of net borrowing cost to be capitalised?
answer_html: Answer: (B) ₹3,30,000 — only the portion of interest attributable to the loan-funded (not grant-funded) part of the qualifying-asset spend is capitalised (loan-funded: building 30 + machinery 20 = 50 out of the total 50 lakh loan, i.e. the entire loan is loan-funded qualifying spend); apportioned against total interest of ₹5,50,000 for the fraction of the year/qualifying use, per AS 16.
topic_text: AS 16 (4.6): Borrowing cost capitalisation restricted to the loan-funded portion of qualifying-asset expenditure

question_html: Which is correct with reference to the subsidy received in the nature of promoters' contribution during 2024-2025: (i) It is not considered as a deferred income. (ii) It is not distributable as a dividend. (iii) It is treated as a capital reserve. (iv) It is not distributable as a dividend but considered as deferred income.
answer_html: Answer: (A) (i), (ii) and (iii) — per AS 12, a grant in the nature of promoters' contribution (given as a proportion of total investment, not related to specific fixed assets, and not in the ordinary course of business) is credited directly to Capital Reserve, treated as shareholders' funds — not as deferred income, and not distributable as a dividend.

question_html: As per AS-26, what is the correct accounting treatment for ₹18 lakhs spent on publicity and research expenses during 2024-2025?

options.A: ₹18 lakhs is treated as an intangible asset and amortised equally over 5 years.
options.B: ₹18 lakhs is treated as an intangible asset and amortised equally over 10 years.
options.C: ₹18 lakhs is treated as goodwill and appears as an asset in the Balance Sheet.
options.D: ₹18 lakhs is charged as an expense in the Statement of Profit and Loss.

answer_html: Answer: (D) — the product failed and generated no future economic benefit, so the full amount is expensed; it never met AS 26's asset-recognition criteria in the first place, and publicity expenditure is expensed as incurred in any case.
topic_text: AS 26 (6.5): Publicity/research expenditure with no resulting future benefit is expensed, never capitalised

question_html: KPK Limited is installing a new Plant: Cost per supplier's invoice ₹45,00,000; Estimated dismantling costs after 5 years ₹3,25,000; Initial operating losses before commercial production ₹4,00,000; Interest paid to supplier for deferred credit ₹2,50,000; Initial delivery and handling costs ₹1,85,000; Cost of site preparation ₹5,00,000; Consultants' fees for acquisition advice ₹6,75,000. What cost can be capitalized for the Plant per AS 10?
answer_html: Answer: (B) ₹61,85,000 — includes invoice cost, dismantling provision, delivery/handling, site preparation, and consultants' fees (all directly attributable to bringing the asset to working condition); excludes initial operating losses before commercial production (expensed, per AS 10) and the deferred-credit interest (a financing cost, not part of acquisition cost unless it qualifies as a borrowing cost under AS 16, which a short supplier-credit arrangement typically does not).
topic_text: AS 10 (2.4): Directly attributable costs capitalised; operating losses before commercial production and deferred-credit interest excluded

question_html: SRS Limited's defined benefit pension plan for the year ended 31st March 2025: Fair market value of plan assets 01.04.24 ₹10,00,000; 31.03.25 ₹14,25,000; Employer Contribution ₹3,50,000; Benefits paid ₹2,50,000. What is the actual return on plan assets per AS-15?
answer_html: Answer: (C) ₹3,25,000 = Closing fair value (14,25,000) − Opening fair value (10,00,000) − Employer contribution (3,50,000) + Benefits paid (2,50,000) = 3,25,000.
topic_text: AS 15 (1.9): Actual return on plan assets - closing less opening fair value, adjusted for contributions in and benefits out

question_html: What is the maximum permissible number of Equity Shares that can be bought back if the Loan Fund is ₹350 Lakhs?
answer_html: Answer: (C) Nil Shares — with Loan Funds at ₹350 lakhs, the Debt-Equity Ratio Test (post-buyback loans cannot exceed twice post-buyback equity) fails at any positive buy-back quantity: shareholders' funds are too small relative to the ₹350 lakh loan for any buy-back to keep the ratio within 2:1, making the permissible quantity Nil under this scenario.

question_html: A dealer in machinery, Shakti Equipments Pvt. Ltd., leased out one of its machines to Delta Tools Ltd. on a 3-year operating lease, with equal annual lease rentals intended to yield a 20% profit margin on the cost of the machinery (₹3,00,000). Economic life of the machinery is 5 years; total expected output over its useful life: Year I 50,000 units, Year II 60,000, Year III 40,000, Year IV 65,000, Year V 85,000. Delta Tools will use the machine for Years I–III only, then return it. Compute the annual lease rent that provides the dealer a 20% profit margin on cost.
answer_html: Answer: (B) ₹60,000. Total amount the dealer targets recovering over the machine's full economic life = cost + 20% margin = ₹3,00,000 × 1.20 = ₹3,60,000. Since this is an operating lease, the dealer recovers this target progressively, in proportion to how much of the machine's total lifetime output/value is consumed during each period of use — not by amortising the full amount over just the 3-year lease term. Output during the 3-year lease (Years I–III): 50,000+60,000+40,000 = 1,50,000 units, exactly 50% of the machine's total 5-year output (3,00,000 units). The dealer therefore targets recovering 50% of ₹3,60,000 = ₹1,80,000 during this lease, as equal annual rentals over the 3 years: ₹1,80,000 / 3 = ₹60,000/year.
topic_text: AS 19 (5.2): Operating lessor's target rental recovery apportioned by the leased asset's output consumed during the lease term, out of its full economic-life output

case_facts_html:
RTS Ltd, ("RTS" or the "Company"), is engaged in the business of manufacturing of equipment/components. The Company has a contract with the Indian Railways for a brake component which is structured such that:

  • The Company's obligation is to deliver the component to the Railways' stockyard, while the delivery terms are ex-works, the Company is responsible for engaging a transporter for delivery.
  • Railways sends an order for a defined quantity.
  • The Company manufactures the required quantity and informs Railways for carrying out the inspection.
  • Railways representatives visit the Company's factory and inspect the components and mark each component with a quality check sticker.
  • Goods once inspected by Railways are marked with a hologram sticker to earmark for delivery identification by the customer when they are delivered to the customer's location.
  • The Company raises an invoice once it dispatches the goods.

The management of RTS is under discussion with the auditors of the Company in respect of accounting of a critical matter as regards its accounting with respect subsequent events i.e. events after the reporting period. They have been checking as to which one of the following events after the reporting period provides evidence of conditions that existed at the end of the reporting period?

  1. Nationalisation or privatization by government
  2. Out of court settlement of a legal claim
  3. Rights issue of equity shares
  4. Strike by workforce
  5. Announcing a plan to discontinue an operation

The Company has received a grant of ₹8 crores from the Government for setting up a factory in a backward area. Out of this grant, the Company distributed ₹2 crores as dividend. The Company also received land, free of cost, from the State Government but it has not recorded this at all in the books as no money has been spent.

RTS has a subsidiary, A Ltd, which is evaluating its production process wherein normal waste is 5% of input. 5,000 MT of input were put in process resulting in wastage of 300 MT. Cost per MT of input was ₹1,000. The entire quantity of waste was on stock at the end of the financial year.
question_html: When should RTS Ltd recognize revenue as per the Accounting Standards notified under the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2006? Would your answer be different if inspection is normally known to lead to no quality rejections?

options.A: Revenue should be recognized on dispatch of components. The assessment would not change even in case where inspection is normally known to lead to no quality rejections.
options.B: Revenue should be recognized on completion of inspection of components. The assessment would not change even in case where inspection is normally known to lead to no quality rejections.
options.C: Revenue should be recognized on dispatch of components. The assessment would change where inspection is normally known to lead to no quality rejections.
options.D: Revenue should be recognized on delivery of the component to the Railways' stockyard. The assessment would change where inspection is normally known to lead to no quality rejections.

answer_html: Answer: (B). Under AS 9, revenue on the sale of goods is recognised only once the seller has transferred the significant risks and rewards of ownership, and no significant uncertainty remains over the consideration or its collectability. Here, Railways' inspection and the affixing of the quality-check/hologram sticker is a substantive condition of the contract, not a formality — until inspection is complete, RTS still bears the risk that the components could be rejected. Revenue is therefore recognised only on completion of inspection, not on mere dispatch or delivery to the stockyard. This conclusion does not change even if inspection is normally known to result in no rejections, because the contractual right of inspection/rejection still exists as a matter of fact until it is actually exercised — a historical track record of passing inspection does not itself transfer the risk earlier.
topic_text: AS 9 — Revenue Recognition (2.4-2.5): Timing of revenue recognition on sale of goods - transfer of significant risks/rewards, inspection as a substantive condition of sale

The management of RTS is under discussion with the auditors of the Company in respect of accounting of a critical matter as regards its accounting with respect subsequent events i.e. events after the reporting period. They have been checking as to which one of the following events after the reporting period provides evidence of conditions that existed at the end of the reporting period?

  3. Rights issue of equity shares
  4. Strike by workforce

The Company has received a grant of ₹8 crores from the Government for setting up a factory in a backward area. Out of this grant, the Company distributed ₹2 crores as dividend. The Company also received land, free of cost, from the State Government but it has not recorded this at all in the books as no money has been spent.

RTS has a subsidiary, A Ltd, which is evaluating its production process wherein normal waste is 5% of input. 5,000 MT of input were put in process resulting in wastage of 300 MT. Cost per MT of input was ₹1,000. The entire quantity of waste was on stock at the end of the financial year.
question_html: In respect of A Ltd, state with reference to Accounting Standards notified under the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2006, what would be value of the inventory to be recorded in the books of accounts?
answer_html: Answer: (D) ₹49,47,368. Total process cost = 5,000 MT × ₹1,000 = ₹50,00,000. Normal waste = 5% of input = 250 MT, absorbed into the cost of good production (no separate value). Abnormal waste = actual waste 300 MT − normal waste 250 MT = 50 MT, valued separately at the normal-unit rate and excluded from inventory. Cost per unit of good output = ₹50,00,000 ÷ (5,000 − 250) = ₹50,00,000 ÷ 4,750 = ₹1,052.6316/MT. Good output = 5,000 − 300 = 4,700 MT. Value of inventory = 4,700 × ₹1,052.6316 = ₹49,47,368 (rounded).
topic_text: AS 2 — Valuation of Inventories (1.9): Normal loss absorbed into cost of good production; abnormal loss valued separately and excluded from inventory

The Company has received a grant of ₹8 crores from the Government for setting up a factory in a backward area. Out of this grant, the Company distributed ₹2 crores as dividend. The Company also received land, free of cost, from the State Government but it has not recorded this at all in the books as no money has been spent.

RTS has a subsidiary, A Ltd, which is evaluating its production process wherein normal waste is 5% of input. 5,000 MT of input were put in process resulting in wastage of 300 MT. Cost per MT of input was ₹1,000. The entire quantity of waste was on stock at the end of the financial year.
question_html: Please guide regarding the accounting treatment of both the grants mentioned above in line with the requirements of Accounting Standard 12.

options.A: Distribution of dividend out of grant is correct. In the second case also not recording land in the books of accounts is correct.
options.B: Distribution of dividend out of grant is incorrect. In the second case, not recording land in the books of accounts is correct.
options.C: Distribution of dividend out of grant is correct. In the second case, land should be recorded in the books of accounts at a nominal value.
options.D: Distribution of dividend out of grant is incorrect. In the second case, land should be recorded in the books of accounts at a nominal value.

answer_html: Answer: (D). The ₹8 crore grant for setting up a factory in a backward area is a grant in the nature of promoters' contribution — per AS 12 it must be credited directly to Capital Reserve and is neither available for distribution as dividend nor treated as deferred income; distributing ₹2 crore of it as dividend is therefore incorrect. Separately, land received free of cost from the State Government is a non-monetary government grant; AS 12 requires such assets to be recorded at their acquisition cost, or at a nominal value if received free of cost — it cannot simply be left off the books because no money was spent.
topic_text: AS 12 — Accounting for Government Grants (1.5/1.8): Grants of the nature of promoters' contribution go to Capital Reserve, not dividend; non-monetary grants received free are recorded at nominal value, not left unrecorded

question_html: Gyan Ltd. borrowed ₹10 crore for construction of a plant at the rate of 10% per annum (interest paid annually ₹1 crore). The construction was being carried on and out of the borrowings, ₹4 crore was temporarily placed in a fixed deposit at the rate of 6% per annum (interest earned ₹24 lakh). At the year end, how much cost of borrowing Gyan Limited will capitalise?

options.A: Interest paid on ₹10 crore i.e. ₹1 crore
options.B: Interest paid on ₹6 crore as only this amount was utilized i.e. ₹60 Lakh.
options.C: Interest paid less income on temporary investment i.e. ₹76 lakh

answer_html: Answer: (C) ₹76 lakh. Per AS 16, where funds are borrowed specifically for a qualifying asset, any income earned on temporary investment of those borrowed funds pending their use is deducted from the borrowing cost otherwise eligible for capitalisation. Interest paid = ₹1 crore (₹100 lakh); less income on the temporary investment of the unused ₹4 crore = ₹24 lakh; net eligible borrowing cost = ₹100 lakh − ₹24 lakh = ₹76 lakh.
topic_text: AS 16 — Borrowing Costs (4.4): Income on temporary investment of surplus borrowed funds is netted against interest paid to arrive at capitalisable borrowing cost

question_html: In the books of G Ltd., closing inventory as at 31.03.2024 amounts to ₹10,40,000 (on the basis of FIFO method). The company decides to change from FIFO method to weighted average method for ascertaining the cost of inventory for 31.3.2024. On the basis of weighted average method, closing inventory as on 31.03.2024 amounts to ₹8,80,000. Realisable value of the inventory as on 31.03.2024 amounts to ₹12,00,000. What will be the value of inventory in the books and what disclosure should be given in the financial statement on 31.3.2024?

options.A: The value of inventory will be ₹8,80,000 and the fact that the valuation method has changed to be disclosed in the financial statement.
options.B: The value of inventory will be ₹12,00,000, and full disclosure with the amount the valuation method has changed to be disclosed in the financial statement.
options.C: The value of inventory will be ₹12,00,000, and the fact that valuation method has changed to be disclosed in the financial statement.
options.D: The value of inventory will be ₹8,80,000, and full disclosure with the amount the valuation method has changed to be disclosed in the financial statement.

answer_html: Answer: (d) The value of inventory will be ₹8,80,000, and full disclosure with the amount the valuation method has changed to be disclosed in the financial statement. Per AS 2, inventory is valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value; once the company changes its costing method to weighted average, the "cost" figure to compare against NRV is the new weighted-average cost of ₹8,80,000, which is lower than the ₹12,00,000 NRV – so ₹8,80,000 is the value in the books. Separately, per AS 5, a change in the cost formula used for inventories is a change in accounting policy, which requires disclosure of both the fact of the change and, where the effect is material, the amount by which the change affects the financial statements.
topic_text: AS 2 — Valuation of Inventories (1.3): Lower of cost and NRV, applied to the newly-adopted cost formula after a change in accounting policy

question_html: A Ltd. has a balance of ₹17,15,000 in the loan account with State Finance Corporation which is inclusive of ₹1,15,000 for interest accrued but not due. The loan is secured by hypothecation of the Plant and Machinery. As per Schedule III to the Companies Act, 2013 loan is to be disclosed in the balance sheet as follows:

options.A: Disclosed ₹16,00,000 as a secured loan under long-term borrowings.
options.B: Disclosed ₹16,00,000 as a secured loan under long-term borrowings and ₹1,15,000 under short-term borrowings.
options.C: Disclosed ₹16,00,000 as a secured loan under long-term borrowings and ₹1,15,000 under other current liabilities.
options.D: Disclosed ₹16,00,000 as a secured loan under long-term borrowings and no disclosure for ₹1,15,000.

answer_html: Answer: (c) Disclosed ₹16,00,000 as a secured loan under long-term borrowings and ₹1,15,000 under other current liabilities. The principal loan balance (₹17,15,000 − ₹1,15,000 interest accrued but not due = ₹16,00,000) is a long-term secured borrowing. Per Schedule III's format, "interest accrued but not due on borrowings" is not itself a borrowing (long-term or short-term) – it is separately classified under "Other current liabilities."
topic_text: Preparation of Financial Statements (1.5): Interest accrued but not due on borrowings is classified under Other Current Liabilities, separate from the borrowing itself

question_html: Most by-products as well as scrap or waste materials, by their nature, are immaterial. Thus, these are measured at:

options.B: Cost or Net Realisable Value whichever is lower

answer_html: Answer: (d) Net realisable value. Per AS 2, because by-products, scrap and waste are immaterial by nature, they are measured at net realisable value, and this NRV is deducted from the cost of the main product(s) rather than being separately costed.
topic_text: AS 2 — Valuation of Inventories (1.7): By-products, scrap and waste, being immaterial, are valued at net realisable value

case_facts_html:
Year 1 - A Company purchased a land from its own funds and started construction on two towers on the land. The Company for the construction borrowed funds of ₹60 lakhs each for both the towers. The Company is required to pay interest of ₹60,000 annually for each loan. During the first year the Company allotted the vacant area for parking purposes which fetched revenue of ₹15,000 in year 1 only. Tower 1 got ready at the end of year 2. The Company capitalised the same and started using the same for intended purpose.

Based on the information given in above Case Scenario, answer Question No. 1 (i)–(iv).
question_html: How much borrowing cost is eligible for capitalisation at the end of year 3:
answer_html: Answer: (a) ₹60,000 — only Tower 2's loan interest remains eligible for capitalisation in year 3, Tower 1 being complete.
topic_text: AS 16 — Borrowing Costs (4.4): Borrowing costs eligible for capitalisation on the still-incomplete tower only

question_html: Suraj Ltd. (the lessee) acquires machinery on lease from Chand Ltd. (the lessor) on April 1, 2025 for 3 years. The economic life of machinery is also 3 years. The fair value of the machinery is ₹2,50,000 and the guaranteed residual value is ₹2,000. As per the lease agreement, the lessee is required to pay ₹1,00,000 per year from April 1, 2025. The lessor has guaranteed a residual value of ₹20,000. However, lessor estimates that it would have a value of ₹5,000 only after 3 years. At what value the machinery would be recognised.
answer_html: Answer: (c) ₹2,37,400 approx.
topic_text: AS 19 — Leases (5.8): Finance lease - lessee's initial recognition at lower of fair value and PV of minimum lease payments

question_html: Which of the following is not an example of cash and cash equivalent balances held by the entity that are not available for use?

options.B: balance in bank account as Fixed deposits
options.C: earmarked bank balances for specific purposes. Examples: bank account for debenture redemption, dividend payment etc.
options.D: balance in bank account subject to legal restrictions.

answer_html: Answer: (b).
topic_text: Cash Flow Statement (2.2): Elements of cash - restricted/earmarked vs freely available balances

question_html: Following is the example of research activities as per AS 26 which is recognised as expense when it is incurred:

options.A: the design, construction and testing of pre-production or pre-use prototypes and models.
options.B: the search for alternatives for materials, devices, products, processes, systems or services.
options.C: the design of tools, jigs, moulds and dies involving new technology.
options.D: the design, construction and operation of a pilot plant that is not of a scale economically feasible for commercial production.

answer_html: Answer: (b) — the search for alternatives for materials, devices, products, processes, systems or services is a Research Phase activity under AS 26 and is always expensed; options (a), (c), and (d) are Development Phase activities.
topic_text: AS 26 — Intangible Assets (6.14): Research Phase - no intangible asset ever recognised, always expensed

case_facts_html:
Suman Ltd. is in the business of manufacturing electronics equipment and selling these at its various outlets. It provides installation services for the equipment sold and also provide free 1 year warranty on all the sold products.

Beach Resorts are leading resorts in the city. It purchased 5 air conditioners (AC) from Suman Ltd. for its resort. Suman Ltd. sold 5 AC to Beach resort for ₹45,000 each which includes installation fees of ₹1,000 for each AC. The Company also offers 1 year warranty for any repair etc. The Company also offered ₹500 per AC as trade discount. Beach resort placed order on March 15, 2024 and made payment on March 20, 2024. The ACs were delivered on March 27, 2024 and the installation was completed on April 5, 2024.
question_html: How much revenue should be recognised by the Company as on March 31, 2024:
answer_html: Answer: (ii) ₹2,17,500. Per unit, the invoice price of ₹45,000 includes an installation fee of ₹1,000, so the equipment-sale component is ₹44,000; the ₹500 trade discount is deducted from this equipment price (trade discounts are deducted in determining revenue, not recognised separately — see Q1(c)), leaving ₹43,500 per AC. Delivery, and hence transfer of the significant risks and rewards of the AC itself, occurred on March 27, 2024, so ₹43,500 × 5 = ₹2,17,500 of equipment revenue is recognised as on March 31, 2024. The separately-priced installation fee is not yet recognised, since installation (a distinct service performed by Suman Ltd. itself) was not completed until April 5, 2024.
topic_text: AS 9 (2.8): Goods subject to installation - deferral of the installation-linked portion of revenue until installation is complete

Beach Resorts are leading resorts in the city. It purchased 5 air conditioners (AC) from Suman Ltd. for its resort. Suman Ltd. sold 5 AC to Beach resort for ₹45,000 each which includes installation fees of ₹1,000 for each AC. The Company also offers 1 year warranty for any repair etc. The Company also offered ₹500 per AC as trade discount. Beach resort placed order on March 15, 2024 and made payment on March 20, 2024. The ACs were delivered on March 27, 2024 and the installation was completed on April 5, 2024.
question_html: How much revenue should be recognised by the Company in the financial year 2024-25:
answer_html: Answer: (i) ₹5,000. The installation fee of ₹1,000 per AC (unaffected by the trade discount, which applies to the equipment price) is recognised as revenue only once installation is actually complete — April 5, 2024, which falls in FY 2024-25. ₹1,000 × 5 ACs = ₹5,000.
topic_text: AS 9 (2.8): Installation-fee revenue recognised in the period installation is actually completed

case_facts_html:
Suman Ltd. is in the business of manufacturing electronics equipment and selling these at its various outlets. It provides installation services for the equipment sold and also provide free 1 year warranty on all the sold products.

Beach Resorts are leading resorts in the city. It purchased 5 air conditioners (AC) from Suman Ltd. for its resort. Suman Ltd. sold 5 AC to Beach resort for ₹45,000 each which includes installation fees of ₹1,000 for each AC. The Company also offers 1 year warranty for any repair etc. The Company also offered ₹500 per AC as trade discount. Beach resort placed order on March 15, 2024 and made payment on March 20, 2024. The ACs were delivered on March 27, 2024 and the installation was completed on April 5, 2024.
question_html: What will be the accounting for trade discount:

options.A: The same will be recognised separately in the profit and loss.
options.B: The trade discounts are deducted in determining the revenue.
options.C: Trade discount will be recognised after one year, when the warranty will be over.
options.D: Trade discount will be recognised after installation is complete.

answer_html: Answer: (ii) The trade discounts are deducted in determining the revenue. Per AS 9, trade discounts and volume rebates are deducted in arriving at the revenue figure — they are never recognised as a separate profit and loss item, and have no connection to the warranty period or the installation date.
topic_text: AS 9 (2.8): Trade discounts deducted in determining revenue, not recognised separately

Suman Ltd. is in the business of manufacturing electronics equipment and selling these at its various outlets. It provides installation services for the equipment sold and also provide free 1 year warranty on all the sold products.

Beach Resorts are leading resorts in the city. It purchased 5 air conditioners (AC) from Suman Ltd. for its resort. Suman Ltd. sold 5 AC to Beach resort for ₹45,000 each which includes installation fees of ₹1,000 for each AC. The Company also offers 1 year warranty for any repair etc. The Company also offered ₹500 per AC as trade discount. Beach resort placed order on March 15, 2024 and made payment on March 20, 2024. The ACs were delivered on March 27, 2024 and the installation was completed on April 5, 2024.
question_html: Is the Company required to do any accounting for 1 year warranty provided by it:

options.A: No accounting treatment is required till some warranty claim is actually received by the Company.
options.B: As there exist a present obligation to provide warranty to customers for 1 year, the Company should estimate the amount that it may have to incur considering various factors including past trends and create a provision as per AS 29.
options.C: Accounting for claims will be done on cash basis i.e. expense will be recognised when expense is made.
options.D: As the Company is not charging separately for the warranty provided, there is no need to create any provision.

answer_html: Answer: (ii) As there exist a present obligation to provide warranty to customers for 1 year, the Company should estimate the amount that it may have to incur considering various factors including past trends and create a provision as per AS 29. The free 1-year warranty is a present obligation arising from a past event (the sale), with a probable outflow of resources and a reliable estimate obtainable from past claims experience — all three AS 29 recognition conditions are met, regardless of whether the warranty is priced separately or bundled into the sale price.
chapter_label: AS 29: Provisions, Contingent Liabilities and Contingent Assets
topic_text: AS 29 (2.4): Present obligation from a past event triggers a provision, estimated using past trends

question_html: As per AS 2, Inventories include materials awaiting use in production process, what should be included in Inventories from the following:

options.A: Secondary Packing material required for transporting and forwarding the material.
options.B: Spare parts, servicing equipment and standby equipment
options.C: Primary packing material which is essential to bring an item of inventory to its saleable condition, for example, bottles, cans etc., in case of food and beverages industry.

answer_html: Answer: (c) Primary packing material which is essential to bring an item of inventory to its saleable condition, for example, bottles, cans etc., in case of food and beverages industry. AS 2 includes in the cost of inventories all costs necessary to bring the item to its present location and saleable condition — primary packaging (e.g. the bottle/can itself) meets this test. Secondary packing (for onward transport) and publicity material are distribution/selling costs, expensed as incurred rather than inventoried; spare parts, servicing equipment and standby equipment are generally accounted for as property, plant and equipment under AS 10, not as inventory.
topic_text: AS 2 (1.2): Scope of inventories - primary packing material necessary to reach saleable condition is includible; spare parts/standby equipment and publicity/secondary-packing costs generally are not

case_facts_html: Surat Ltd. has received a grant of ₹40 crore for purchase of a qualified machine costing ₹90 crores. Residual value ₹2 crore, useful life 20 years, straight-line depreciation. Answer the following per AS 12, Government Grants.
question_html: What is the nature of the Grant being received by Surat Ltd.?

options.B: Grant related to specific fixed assets

answer_html: Answer: (ii) Grant related to specific fixed assets — the grant was given specifically for the purchase of the qualified machine.
topic_text: AS 12 (1.2): Classifying a grant given specifically for a named asset as a grant related to specific fixed assets

case_facts_html: Surat Ltd. has received a grant of ₹40 crore for purchase of a qualified machine costing ₹90 crores. Residual value ₹2 crore, useful life 20 years, straight-line depreciation. Answer the following per AS 12, Government Grants.
question_html: If Surat Ltd. has the policy to recognise the grant as a deduction from the cost of the asset, what will be the amount of depreciation charged as expense every year?
answer_html: Answer: (iii) ₹2.4 crores = [(90−40 grant)−2 residual] / 20 years = (50−2)/20 = 48/20 = 2.4.
topic_text: AS 12 (1.4): Grant deducted from asset cost - depreciation charged on the net (grant-reduced) depreciable amount

case_facts_html: Surat Ltd. has received a grant of ₹40 crore for purchase of a qualified machine costing ₹90 crores. Residual value ₹2 crore, useful life 20 years, straight-line depreciation. Answer the following per AS 12, Government Grants.
question_html: If Surat Ltd. has the policy to recognise the grant as deferred income, what amount of grant will be recognised as other income every year?
answer_html: Answer: (iii) ₹2 crores = grant ₹40 crores recognised as income over the asset's 20-year useful life on a systematic basis matching depreciation: 40/20 = 2 crores/year.
topic_text: AS 12 (1.5): Deferred-income approach - grant recognised as income systematically over the asset's useful life

case_facts_html: Surat Ltd. has received a grant of ₹40 crore for purchase of a qualified machine costing ₹90 crores. Residual value ₹2 crore, useful life 20 years, straight-line depreciation. Answer the following per AS 12, Government Grants.
question_html: If Surat Ltd. has the policy to recognise the grant as deferred income, what will be the amount of depreciation charged as expense every year?
answer_html: Answer: (ii) ₹4.4 crores — under the deferred-income approach, the asset is carried at its full gross cost (not reduced by the grant), so depreciation is computed on the gross depreciable amount: (90−2)/20 = 88/20 = 4.4.
topic_text: AS 12 (1.5): Deferred-income approach - depreciation computed on the full (un-reduced) gross cost of the asset

question_html: In G Ltd.'s books, closing inventory at 31.03.2024 was ₹10,40,000 (FIFO method). The company changes to weighted average method for 31.3.2024: closing inventory becomes ₹8,80,000. Realisable value at 31.03.2024 is ₹12,00,000. What will be the value of inventory in the books and what disclosure should be given?

options.A: The value will be ₹8,80,000 and the fact that the valuation method has changed to be disclosed.
options.B: The value will be ₹12,00,000, and full disclosure with the amount the valuation method has changed to be disclosed.
options.C: The value will be ₹12,00,000, and the fact that the valuation method has changed to be disclosed.
options.D: The value will be ₹8,80,000, and full disclosure with the amount the valuation method has changed to be disclosed.

answer_html: Answer: (iv) — inventory is valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value; the weighted-average cost (₹8,80,000) is lower than NRV (₹12,00,000), so ₹8,80,000 is the book value. Since this is a change in accounting policy (costing formula) with a material effect, AS 1/AS 2 require full disclosure, including the quantified amount of the effect of the change (not merely the fact of the change).
topic_text: AS 2 (1.2): Change in cost formula requires full disclosure of the change and its quantified financial effect

question_html: Cost of a current investment acquired was ₹1000 but fair value was ₹800; recorded at ₹800. Now fair value of the investment is ₹1200. At what value should it be recorded, and how much gain credited to profit and loss?

options.B: Recorded at ₹1000 and gain of ₹200 credited to P&L.
options.C: Recorded at ₹1200 and gain of ₹400 credited to P&L.
options.D: Recorded at ₹1200 but no gain credited to P&L.

answer_html: Answer: (ii) — current investments are carried at the lower of cost and fair value; even though fair value has now risen to ₹1,200 (above cost), the investment cannot be marked up beyond its original cost of ₹1,000. The carrying value is restored from ₹800 to ₹1,000 (the ceiling), recognising a gain of ₹200 (1,000−800) — the further rise from 1,000 to 1,200 is unrealised and not recognised.
topic_text: AS 13 (3.3): Current investments carried at the lower of cost and fair value - never marked up beyond original cost
